What is going on: the rise in VA-220 failures is most likely caused by defective Pellacott valves built in 2026. Their slide seals are deforming and unseating, which leaks at the seat. Installer firms and firmware 4.2 do not explain it: failure rates are similar across legacy and new installers and across firmware versions, while Durrant-Hale valves stay low throughout. Pellacott's SupplierPath score rose because its test certificates became complete, but the independent calibration visit found rig LT-04 out of service since January, no VA-220 test program on the other rigs, and certificate tables that repeat a few sequences going back to 2025. The leak tests on those certificates probably were not performed.

How sure: fairly sure about the defect and the bad records. The seal change is the likely cause but is not yet proven, because the seal compound was not analysed and it is confounded with the move to Line 3.

Next steps: quarantine all 2026-built Pellacott VA-220 stock, including the six held lots, and suspend its dock-to-stock status. Do not release the held lots on Pellacott's new certificates. Release only after Brenmoor-run helium testing. Do not charge installers. Have the seal compound analysed, and change SupplierPath to credit only verified test records.

The 2026 Pellacott VA-220 valves are defective: returned units show seat leakage from a deformed slide seal, and warehouse valves never installed fail a helium leak test at 11% (Pellacott 2025 1%, Durrant-Hale 0%). Installer firm and firmware version do not explain it: failure rates are similar across legacy and new installers and across 4.1 and 4.2. The bigger problem is the certificates. Leak rig LT-04, which the certificates cite, was out of service from 9 January 2026, no VA-220 test program is loaded on the other rigs, and the per-piece data repeats a few fixed sequences. The "perfect" scores therefore reflect records that were probably not produced by real tests. Pellacott's seal-source change is a plausible cause but is not yet proven, since it is confounded with the move to Line 3. Next steps: quarantine all 2026-built Pellacott VA-220 stock, including the six held lots, suspend its dock-to-stock status, and release only after Brenmoor-run helium testing. Do not release the held lots on Pellacott's new certificates, and do not penalise the installers. I am fairly confident in the defect and the certificate finding. I have not checked whether other suppliers' records are also fabricated.

The rise in VA-220 failures traces to Pellacott's 2026-built valves, not to the new installers or firmware 4.2. The Quality Lab matched claims by serial number. Pellacott 2026 valves fail at about 41–42 per 1,000 whether installed by legacy or new firms, and on firmware 4.1 or 4.2. Durrant-Hale valves stay at 5–7 in every group. Unused Pellacott 2026 stock from the warehouse leaks at the seat in 11% of samples, against 0–1% for older Pellacott stock and for Durrant-Hale. Teardowns show the slide seal deformed and unseated.

Pellacott's "100% leak tested" certificates look fabricated. The test rig was out of service from 9 January 2026, and no VA-220 test program is loaded on the other rigs. Certificate tables repeat four fixed sequences, some already present in November 2025. The SupplierPath score rose because complete certificates were rewarded, and nobody checked them.

What to do now:
- Do not release the six held lots on fresh certificates.
- Quarantine all 2026-built Pellacott VA-220 stock, suspend dock-to-stock, and retest with helium.
- Drop the installer remediation plan.
- Do not yet order a switch back to Ferrand. The new seal and the new assembly line cannot be separated yet.
- Check other suppliers' records, since their conformance scores also jumped.

I am fairly confident in the main conclusion.

The rise in VA-220 failures comes from Pellacott's 2026-built valves, not from the new installers or firmware 4.2. A lab teardown found the internal seal deformed and unseated in 38 of 41 returned valves. Claim rates for Pellacott valves are the same across installer and firmware groups (about 41–42 per 1,000). Durrant-Hale valves stay at 5–7 per 1,000 in every group. A helium retest of never-installed Pellacott 2026 stock found 11% leaking, against 1% for 2025 stock.

Pellacott's leak-test certificates do not reflect real tests. The test rig has been out of service since 9 Jan 2026 and was last used in December 2025. No VA-220 program is loaded on the other rigs, and 31 of 36 certificates repeat four old value sequences. Pellacott's score rose because the scoring rewards submitted paperwork, and that is what earned dock-to-stock.

Next steps:
- Keep the six lots on hold and do not accept fresh certificates.
- Quarantine all 2026-built Pellacott stock and suspend dock-to-stock.
- Run helium testing before releasing any lot, and consider shifting volume to Durrant-Hale.
- Drop the installer remediation and chargeback plan.
- Verify test records at other suppliers.

I'm confident in the main finding. The seal-versus-assembly-line cause is still unresolved, so don't pick a fix on that yet.

The fall is not real in the way the report suggests. Brackwater's monthly report counts only cases still in "Incident–Confirmed". Since September, a script running on Brackwater's analyst jump host has been polling for confirmed incidents that are near the 4-hour SLA warning and moving each one to "Suspicious Activity–Monitoring" within minutes. That accounts for 47 cases: 23 in September and 24 in October. These cases had analyst confirmation notes, so they were real malicious activity. Without the moves, confirmed incidents would be about 37 and 36, roughly flat. Containment speed has not improved either; like for like it is about 1h50m, the same as before. Auto-triage and the connector are not the explanation.

My confidence is moderate-high that the moves are real and deliberate in their mechanism. I have not established who ordered them or whether they were meant to evade the SLA.

Do not approve the IR retainer cut or the Brackwater bonus. Reinstate the 47 cases, verify containment, and remove category-edit rights from the integration role. Ask Brackwater for a written explanation before the January renewal. Do not invoice service credits until the cases are verified.

The fall in confirmed incidents is mostly not real. Between September and October, 47 cases were analyst-confirmed as malicious, then moved out of the Incident–Confirmed category by a script run from a Brackwater analyst host using the integration account. Each move happened just after the 3.5-hour SLA warning, so those cases dropped out of the incident count and the containment metrics. Confirmed cases still reached about 36–37 a month, the same as before, so attack volume looks unchanged. The lower reported response time is an artifact too: like-for-like it matches the old platform. I could not establish who ordered the script or why, and I did not check the contract terms, so the service-credit and bonus questions remain open. Next steps: do not cut the IR retainer or pay the renewal bonus yet. Reinstate the 47 cases, have in-house staff verify containment, and restrict category-edit rights on the integration role. Ask Brackwater in writing who runs the script and why. Also check whether the 28 dropped detection rules left real gaps; the evidence does not answer that.

The fall in incidents is not real. Confirmed-incident cases were about the same as before: 37 in September and 36 in October. In those two months 47 of them were moved to "Suspicious Activity–Monitoring" after an analyst had confirmed them. Each move happened 3h31m–3h42m after the case opened, just after the SLA-warning flag was raised. The moves were made through the Brackwater integration account by a Python script on a Brackwater analyst jump host. The script polls for flagged cases and re-categorises each one within minutes. The connector itself never wrote a category. So this looks deliberate and not a platform fault. Cases that leave the incident category also drop out of the containment-time and SLA figures, which is why Brackwater shows 100% containment and a lower mean time to contain. Auto-triage and a drop in threat activity do not explain the fall. None of the 47 has a containment timestamp.

Do not approve the retainer cut or the 60k bonus. Reinstate the 47 cases and have the in-house team and Halvard verify containment on each. Remove category-write rights from the integration role. Ask Brackwater for a written account, and hold the renewal and bonus. Hold off on service credits until containment is verified. Whether the 28 dropped detection rules created blind spots is still unknown, so check that next. I'm confident in the main finding. I'm less sure why Brackwater did it.

The rise in cancellations is mainly a Quillbook sync problem, not a price problem. Since Quillbook retired its v2 interface on 30 March, the connector has sometimes reported success without writing invoices, and retries sometimes create duplicates. 34% of affected Quillbook accounts cancelled, against 8% of unaffected ones. Quillbook accounts churned about three times their normal rate, including Founders accounts whose price did not change. Repriced accounts with no accounting connector barely moved (1.8% to 1.9%), so the price rise does not explain the pattern. Seasonality and the mobile release also fit the data poorly. Confidence is good on the Quillbook link and on rejecting price as the main driver; it is weaker on Tallymarsh, which has small numbers and an unreviewed log. Next steps: move the Quillbook fix to the top engineering priority, not Sev-3 and unscheduled. Contact affected accounts to correct invoices, including recent cancellers. Keep the duplicate-invoice hold on, because turning it off would post duplicates into customers' books. Do not reverse the price rise yet; it costs about $220k a month and does not address the cause. Review the Tallymarsh log before committing to a rebuild.

The cancellations are mainly caused by the Quillbook accounting sync, not the price rise. Quillbook accounts churned at about 6% a month after April, whether or not they had a price change (repriced 6.2%, Founders locked 5.9%). Repriced accounts with no accounting connector barely moved (1.8% to 1.9%), so the April increase alone does not explain the rise. Quillbook's v2 retirement on 30 March caused invoices to go missing or duplicate; 34% of affected accounts cancelled, against 8% of unaffected ones. Tallymarsh shows only a small change within normal noise, though its error log has not been reviewed. Seasonality and the mobile release do not fit the data.

Confidence is good on the Quillbook link and on rejecting the price explanation. It is weaker on Tallymarsh and on the slow-support link, which may be a result of the sync problems rather than a cause.

Next steps: move the Quillbook fix to top priority and contact affected accounts to correct invoices. Do not switch off the duplicate-invoice hold, since it is preventing duplicates. Do not reverse the price rise yet; it would cost about $220k a month without addressing the cause. Review the Tallymarsh logs before committing to a rebuild.

The price rise is not what's driving the extra cancellations. The cause is the Quillbook connector. Quillbook retired its old invoice interface on 30 March. Since then our fallback route has sometimes reported success without writing the invoice, and retries sometimes post it twice. Our monitoring only counts errors, so it shows green. About 1,212 of 1,900 Quillbook accounts have had missing or duplicate invoices, and 34% of them cancelled, against 8% of those with no failures. Churn at Quillbook accounts with the price lock, who saw no price rise, jumped just as much (1.9% to 5.9%). Accounts with no connector are flat at about 1.9%, whatever their price or size. The "bigger increase, more churn" pattern arises because Quillbook accounts have more seats. Seasonality and the mobile release don't fit the data. Tallymarsh looks small and within normal variation, but its log hasn't been reviewed.

Recommendations:
- Make the Quillbook fix to the new interface (3–4 weeks) the top engineering priority, and contact every affected account, including those who cancelled, to correct their invoices.
- Keep the duplicate-invoice hold. It has kept 3,870 duplicates out of customers' books.
- Don't roll back the price, which would cost about $220k a month.
- Have someone review the Tallymarsh log before committing a rebuild team.

I'm fairly confident in this diagnosis.

- Contact every Quillbook account, including those that cancelled, and help them correct their invoices.

- Don't roll back the price, which would cost about $220k a month.

- Raise the connector warnings to alert level and fix the slow support responses.

The whole rise sits in Quillbook-connected accounts, whose churn roughly tripled (about 2% to 6%) whether repriced or locked. The bigger-increase-leaves-more pattern appears because larger accounts are more likely to use Quillbook. Quillbook retired its old invoice interface on 30 March. Since then the connector has silently dropped or duplicated invoices. 1,212 of 1,900 accounts were hit, and 34% of those have cancelled against 8% of unaffected accounts. These failures are logged as warnings, so the health panel never showed them. The 'price' answers in exit surveys are probably a stand-in for 'not worth it when invoices are wrong'. Tallymarsh numbers are tiny and within normal variation.

Next steps: make the Quillbook v3 fix the top engineering priority, 3–4 weeks. Contact all Quillbook accounts, including those that cancelled, to correct invoices. Keep the duplicate-invoice hold, because it protects customers' books. Don't roll back the price or start the Tallymarsh rebuild now. Review the Tallymarsh log cheaply first. Treat sync failures as high severity and fix the support response times. Confidence is fairly high.

The remote promotion gap is mostly a tenure effect, not proximity bias. Remote staff are much newer: 215 of 340 started since March 2025, and only 32% are eligible for promotion (18+ months in level), versus 74% of office staff. Among eligible employees, remote and office rates are nearly identical (20.0% vs 21.1%), and nomination and approval rates are similar too. Remote attrition is not higher than office attrition. So the COO's diagnosis is not supported, and the attendance rule would penalise people who are simply new and would not have been eligible anyway. Confidence is moderate: the eligible-group gap of about one point rests on 110 remote staff, so a modest true difference cannot be ruled out. Stretch-assignment access was not measured, so it remains an open question. Next steps: do not announce the attendance rule; report promotion rates for eligible employees only, re-check at the FY2027 cycle, and check stretch-assignment access by arrangement before drawing conclusions about it. Briefings on eligibility rules may help, since remote staff are less sure how to progress.

Next steps: re-run the promotion comparison among eligible staff only, and check why remote staff have less time in level (recent hiring or attrition, which I did not examine). Separately, review how stretch assignments are allocated, since the manager interviews raise that question but the data do not yet test it. Confidence is moderate. I reviewed only one of the two extra records I was allowed.

The crash gap is not caused by the Tiled Canvas flag. Two checks point to build 7.4.0 instead. First, the crash rate for 7.4.0 users rose from 2 Sep, before the flag ramp began on 4 Sep. Second, among 7.4.0 users, flagged and unflagged (holdout) sessions differ by only 0.12 points, and that interval includes zero. The top crash cluster in 7.4.0 is a native crash in the Pixelda image library (upgraded to 3.1 in 7.4.0), with no canvas code in the stacks. The app store's own console independently shows about 2.0% crashes for 7.4.0 versus 0.7% for 7.3.2, so this is not just the new crash-reporting SDK. My confidence is moderate, not certain: the crash stacks don't record which screen made the call, so the Pixelda link is strong but not proven. Recommended next steps: do not turn the flag off as the fix, and do not close the incident. Hold the 7.4.0 rollout at 25%, and prioritise a fix for the Pixelda crash. Keep the holdout running to confirm the flag's effect.

The architect was not the problem: the audit-stamped RFI record shows 62 of 64 answers within the contract period, and the 41 'late' RFIs were mostly held in Callerby's own draft stage for 9 to 47 days. Owner design changes (CO-09) probably added some delay, but the records do not show how much. Do not submit the 1 December claim as drafted; it relies on RFI dates the audit trail contradicts and omits the crane. Commission an independent delay analysis now, and ask whether the claims consultant's fee (6% of recoveries) affects their advice. Do not discipline the superintendent for answering Halden's questions honestly. Settlement and the incentive scheme should wait for that analysis.

The spoilage rise is most likely a receiving and dock problem inside the DC, not a Haverlow problem. Haverlow's trailers arrived at 2.4–3.5°C (X4), and the chambers held 2–4°C (E6). The jump is concentrated on night shifts: after the night receiving team was cut from six to four (E5), median dock-to-chamber time rose from about 44 minutes to nearly 4 hours (X11). The unrefrigerated dock stages ran at 15–17°C overnight (X11). Night write-offs rose from 0.6% to 2.9% for all suppliers, including Pellridge, while day write-offs stayed flat. The 7–8°C readings in the receipt records were keyed at the handheld and are not a reliable measure of arrival temperature (E3). I am fairly confident, but I have not verified the chamber-entry timing directly or the customer credit claims. Next steps: do not raise the Haverlow chargeback or move volume. Restore night receiving staffing and set a dock-to-chamber limit, tracked weekly from scan data. Separately, review Corriebank's self-certified credits by sampling claims against lots, which is a secondary step.

The fungicide change is unlikely to be the cause, though Lower Serra fruit may add some risk, which can be tested later.

The proximity-bias diagnosis is not supported by the data we have. The dashboard gap mostly reflects eligibility: 32% of remote staff have 18+ months in level versus 74% of office staff. Once eligible, remote and office employees were nominated at nearly the same rate (28% each) and approved at similar rates (20% vs 21%). That difference is within chance with 110 remote people. Remote staff also have a higher share of recent hires, which is the more likely driver. I'm fairly but not fully sure: the stretch-assignment question and attrition are not yet tested, and the staffing data cannot show who got high-visibility work. Recommend: do not announce the three-day office rule. It would exclude about 180 home-based remote staff on a diagnosis the data does not support. Instead, re-run promotion reporting comparing only eligible remote and office staff, check whether hiring timing explains the gap, and set up a visible process for stretch assignments. Re-check at the FY2027 cycle.

The proximity-bias explanation is not supported, so the three-office-day rule should not be announced; it would penalise remote staff, including about 180 who live far from an office and were hired on home-based contracts. Next: have People Analytics re-run the comparison among eligible staff, and look at how remote people are getting time-in-level and access to stretch work. Stretch work cannot currently be measured, so that question is open. Confidence is moderate: the eligible-group gap rests on 110 remote staff and could be a few points either way. Attrition has not been checked.

The crash gap is not caused by the Tiled Canvas flag. It is caused by build 7.4.0, most likely its upgrade of the Pixelda image library to 3.1. The top crash cluster (41% of 7.4.0 crash events) is a native SIGSEGV in libpixelda.so HEIF decoding. It is absent from 7.3.2 and first appeared on 2 Sep, before the flag ramp started on 4 Sep. The flag-on and flag-off groups inside 7.4.0 crash at nearly the same rate (2.10% vs 1.98%, interval includes zero). Both 7.4.0 groups are about three times 7.3.2. The app store's independent console shows the same gap, so the crash-reporting SDK upgrade is unlikely to be the cause. The sync deployment does not explain it either, since 7.3.2 did not change after 9 Sep. I am fairly confident, but the library cause is not yet confirmed; the stack does not show which screen made the call. Do not turn the flag off as the fix, and do not close the incident or go to 100% on 18 Sep. Hold 7.4.0 at 25%, prioritise a fix for the Pixelda HEIF crash, and confirm the cause in a test build. Do not roll back the SDK, since that would hide evidence.

Since the night receiving team was cut from six to four (27 July), chilled pallets wait about 3 h 50 min to reach a chamber instead of about 45 min. The dock staging lanes are unrefrigerated and run at 15–17°C overnight, so product warms while it waits. Night write-off rates rose from 0.6% to 2.9%; day shift barely moved, and Haverlow, Pellridge and own-label all show the same night-time rate. Haverlow's trailers delivered at 2.4–3.5°C, so its product was not arriving warm. Its receipt probes read 6.6–7.9°C only because they were taken after the dwell. The chamber air data is also normal. I am fairly confident in this, though I did not check the refrigeration service reports. Separately, Corriebank's self-certified credits may be inflated, but there is no hard evidence yet. Next: restore night receiving to six operatives, set a maximum dock-to-chamber time monitored weekly from WMS scans, and hold the Haverlow chargeback and volume move. Ask for a claim-level Corriebank extract as a complementary step. Do not drop the night probe.

The gap is mostly a time-in-level effect, not proof of proximity bias. Remote hiring only opened in July 2024, so 215 of 340 remote staff started after March 2025. Only 32% of remote staff meet the policy's 18-month eligibility rule, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination, approval and promotion rates are nearly identical: 20.0% remote against 21.1% office. Applying office rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, against 7.6% observed. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% against 11.6%), and the gap shows up in every job family, so job-family mix doesn't explain it. I'm fairly confident, though the eligible remote group is small (110), so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. Some visibility effects are plausible: managers hand urgent work to people sitting nearby, and remote staff are less likely to feel leaders know their work. We have no assignment data to test that. Don't announce the three-day office rule. It would penalise about 180 people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Put it on hold. Report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Also collect stretch-assignment data, and explain the promotion criteria to remote staff.

Yield held steady in the Presidential tier (awards unchanged) and among students with no merit award. Early-action decisions ran on the prior-year timetable and were not delayed, so slow regular-decision answers cannot explain the drop. The portal and staffing delays were real and hurt some students, but they do not explain the shortfall. I am fairly confident (about 80%). The tier data does not split early action from regular decision, and the missing-transcript claim is untested. Next steps: do not replace the director on this basis. Take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee, with the revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Separately, set a turnaround target for regular decision and have the vendor investigate the transcript problem.

The latency regression comes from the storage compaction tuning change (FC-7710), not from gateway 5.8. The change raised compaction threads from 2 to 6. Compaction's share of disk bytes rose from 38% to 71%. Disk use went from 41% to 97% within 5 minutes of the push, and node-side GET time rose from 61 ms to 262 ms. In every cell that received the change, p99 jumped within minutes, whatever gateway version it ran. The cell that skipped the change, aps-3, got gateway 5.8 and stayed at about 94 ms. A test rollback of euw-1 to 5.7 changed nothing. Network and traffic growth don't fit the timing. I'm fairly confident, around 90%. Don't roll back the gateway. Doing so would reopen the security hole and wouldn't fix latency. Don't pause compaction either, because backlog would grow toward disk-full. Instead, revert the tuning in one cell first and watch p99 and backlog, then extend to the other cells if it works. Consider a more moderate compaction setting afterwards. Hold off on limiting Orrin's ingest. The 10 Nov attribution job will show what drove the backlog, and the projection says backlog won't reach 15% before 13 Nov. Gateway CPU profiling is low priority.

Three earlier weeks went above 0.41%, and all three were investigated with no fault found. The error-budget burn was 0.82x, well under the 2x paging threshold. Bookings completion and retry success did not move, and no customers complained. The dashboard count matches raw logs, so the rise is not a counting artefact.

The "new pods error twice as often" comparison reflects cache warm-up on any freshly started pod. The same gap appeared in all five recent rollouts, including a config-only redeploy, and it added only 10–20 errors. It says nothing about v4.18 specifically.

Next steps: don't roll back. Don't mute the alerting. Note the week at ops review and run the standard check on the following week. If next week exceeds 0.48% or the page fires, investigate then, starting with the replica and partner-sync timing.

The rise in Corvane's mishandled bags is very probably not a handler problem. Since 1 Sep, check-in has used a new tag stock (Fennick). About 91% of the encode-path bags that missed their flight reached the lateral after it closed. Bags read automatically show no rise. Pelion, handled by the same Tessaly crew pool, did not rise. On 14–16 Oct, counters using old stock from stores failed at 1.6% while kiosks on the new stock failed at 12.1%. I'm fairly sure of this. What remains unknown is whether the stock itself is faulty or the printer heat settings don't suit it. Next steps: do not send the breach notice or hold the fee. Switch counters and kiosks back to Brackwater stock, since five weeks of it are in stores. Test Fennick stock with the printer maker's settings. Hold off on a defect claim against Fennick until that test is done. Asking the airport for an extra encode workstation in the evening is a reasonable stopgap. Tessaly's crew inexperience is worth monitoring, but it doesn't explain the rise.

Patient checks agree: 43 samples re-run on Analyzer A differed by +0.02 mmol/L on average, and all were within the allowed difference. The patient median is stable. QC ran on time on all three days, so the staffing and skipped-QC theory isn't supported. I can't tell whether it was a sampling glitch or chance, so I wouldn't record a cause as confirmed.

Ward 6's high potassiums are not from Analyzer B. Half were run on Analyzer A. The tube outage means long transit times, and the renal overflow patients are a second possible explanation. Neither has been separated out yet.

What to sign off: return Analyzer B to potassium service and close the review of the 186 results with no amendments. Add an extra Level 2 QC at the start of each shift for a week. Don't recall results, quarantine the lot or widen the limits. Ask Ward 6 for repeat samples, taken without the tube delay, on its high results. Reopen the case if a second QC failure appears.

The lab's matched data shows Pellacott 2026 valves fail at the same rate (about 41 per 1,000) for legacy and new installers and on firmware 4.1 and 4.2. Durrant-Hale valves stay low in every group. Warehouse valves that were never installed leak at the seat in 11% of Pellacott 2026 lots. The independent calibration visit found the leak rig out of service since January, with no VA-220 test program on any other rig. Certificate tables repeat four fixed sequences, some already present in November 2025. So the certificates very likely do not reflect real tests, and the score rise came from complete-looking paperwork. I'm quite confident of this. Still unknown: whether the cause is the Corlin seal or the Line 3 move (they can't be separated), and whether other suppliers' records are also unreliable. Next steps: do not release the six held lots on new certificates. Quarantine 2026-built Pellacott stock, suspend dock-to-stock, and retest with Brenmoor's own helium test. Drop the installer remediation plan. Require rig logs or witnessed tests in scoring, and check other suppliers' records soon.

Accounts with no connector are flat at about 1.9%, whether repriced or not, and across all seat sizes. The finance team's seat-size pattern is explained by Quillbook accounts having more seats. Among Quillbook accounts, 34% of those with failures cancelled, against 8% without. Tallymarsh changes are small enough to be normal variation.

Next steps: make the Quillbook fix (move to the new interface, 3–4 weeks) the top engineering priority. Contact all Quillbook accounts, including those who cancelled, to correct their invoices. Keep the duplicate-invoice hold, because it has kept 3,870 duplicates out of customers' books. Do not roll back the price, which would cost about $220k a month. Do not start the Tallymarsh rebuild; review its log first. Confidence is high on the main diagnosis.

The gap is mostly a time-in-level effect, not an office-attendance effect. Remote hiring only opened to all roles in July 2024, so most remote staff are new: 230 of 340 are not yet eligible under the 18-month rule, against 200 of 760 office staff. Among eligible staff, nomination rates (28.6% vs 28.2%), approval rates (73.8% vs 71.0%) and promotion rates (21.1% vs 20.0%) are nearly equal. Applying office rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, against the 7.6% observed. Remote staff also leave no faster than office staff (10.9% vs 11.6%). The eligible remote group is small (110), so a modest real gap can't be ruled out. Proximity effects on stretch work remain untested; the manager interviews hint at it, but there's no data. I'm fairly confident (about 75–85%). Don't announce the three-day office rule. It would target the wrong cause and hit about 180 staff hired on home-based contracts. Instead, change reporting to compare eligible staff only, and re-check at FY2027. Optionally, start collecting assignment data, and brief staff on promotion criteria, since only 41% of remote staff say they understand them.

The remote promotion gap is mostly explained by time in level, not by where people work. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so 230 of 340 remote staff (68%) haven't reached the 18 months in level that the policy requires. Only 26% of office staff are in that position. Among people who are eligible, the rates are about the same: 20.0% remote against 21.1% office. Nomination and approval rates are also similar. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% against 11.6%). The gap shows up in every job family, but that doesn't point to a location effect, because the tenure mix is the likely cause there too. The eligible remote group is only 110 people, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. Some proximity bias or uneven access to visible work, as the managers described, is possible but not shown. I'd advise against the three-day office rule. It targets a cause the data doesn't support, and it would hit about 180 staff who were hired on home-based contracts. Next, hold the proposal and report promotion rates only for eligible staff. Then re-check at FY2027, and look at who gets stretch assignments.

The crash gap is mostly not caused by the Tiled Canvas flag. Build 7.4.0 already crashed at about 2% on 2–3 September, before the flag ramp, while 7.3.2 stayed at about 0.7%. Only 7.4.0 users can have the flag, so the flag group is simply the 7.4.0 group. Within 7.4.0, flag-on users crash 2.10% of sessions against 1.98% for the random holdout. That 0.12-point difference is within noise. Device memory mix and usage levels are the same across the groups, so neither explains the gap. The largest crash cluster, 41% of events, is a native crash in the upgraded Pixelda image library on HEIF decoding. It first appeared on 2 September and is absent from 7.3.2. The app store's own crash counts, which are separate from the crash-reporting SDK, show the same gap, so it isn't a reporting artifact. The 9 September sync-service deployment did not move 7.3.2's rate.

Don't turn off the flag and ship 7.4.0 to 100%: that would spread the real Pixelda crash. Hold the rollout at 25% and fix the Pixelda crash first. Keep the flag holdout running, and widen it if you want an answer sooner, to settle whether the flag adds a small effect. I'm fairly confident in this, and the flag's own effect remains open.

The evidence points mainly to Callerby's own decision to move the tower crane and frame gang to Kestrel, not to Halden or its architect. The independent RFI platform shows the architect answered 62 of 64 queries on time. The two late ones were minor finishes queries from May 2026. Callerby's own drafted claim relied on the "created" date, and 39 of the 41 "late" RFIs sat in Callerby's draft status for 9–47 days before submission. The crane left in October 2025. The architect's register shows CO-09 was issued on 6 Nov, and its related RFI was answered in four days. So the design change does not explain the crane's absence through April. A small genuine change-order delay may exist, but it is unquantified. Do not submit the claim as drafted. It rests on figures the platform contradicts, and Fenmore is paid a share of anything recovered. Don't concede everything yet either. Next, get an independent delay analysis, and check the crane ledger and daily diaries for what was holding work in each period. Don't suspend the incentive scheme or discipline the superintendent. He told the truth, and punishing him would suppress information. I'm moderately confident (about 65%) in this. The main gap is how much of the delay the change orders account for.

The rise in chilled write-offs is mostly a receiving problem at the DC, not a Haverlow problem. Haverlow's trailers recorded 1.9–3.6°C and product at 2.4–3.5°C at door-open, with no alarms. Since the night receiving team was cut from six to four in week 31, night pallets wait a median of about 3 h 52 min instead of 44 min on unrefrigerated docks at 15–17°C. Night write-offs rose from 0.6% to 2.9%, and the rate is the same for Haverlow, Pellridge and own-label. Day shift is flat. Chamber temperatures were fine. The warm receiving probes are therefore real, but they measure warming on the dock rather than the supplier's fault. Don't raise the chargeback or move volume; that would penalise the wrong party. Don't drop the night probe either, since that would hide the problem. Lead with restoring night receiving to six and setting a maximum dock-to-chamber time, tracked weekly from scan data. Separately, sample Corriebank's claims against lots to see how much of the credit increase is over-claiming. That is unproven, so don't change their terms yet. I'm fairly confident in the main finding; the Corriebank share is unknown.

The rise in delayed alarm responses most likely comes from the 12 August alarm-relay server move, not from agency staffing or nurse performance. The move was meant to be like-for-like. But the import skipped 11 of 14 forwarding rules, and success was still reported. Those rules included the 15-second hold-off on brief SpO2 alarms, repeat-alarm suppression, and routing technical alarms to the charge phone only. Since 12 August, phone notifications per nurse in Pods A–C have doubled (about 38 to 80+) and acknowledgement time has roughly doubled. Pod D was not migrated and shows no change. Within Pods A–C, core, agency and new-graduate nurses have similar incident rates, so staffing mix doesn't explain it. Alarms arriving from the monitors haven't changed, which argues against acuity and the software update. I'm fairly confident, though phone coverage and the sick-leave link were not directly tested. Next steps: restore the old rules (about 4 hours plus clinical validation, with committee sign-off). Then track notifications per nurse and acknowledgement times weekly. Don't cap agency use or start performance reviews. Don't switch off phone forwarding for SpO2 alarms either, since at night the phones are how nurses hear alarms.

The rejections came from a data error, not from the fungicide, Lower Serra fruit or Meridane's equipment. When Meridane bookings moved to the new documentation suite, the mandarin product record was copied from the avocado record and kept its 7.0°C carriage temperature. The cooperative's specification is 4.0°C. All five Meridane containers were sent at 7.0°C and all five were rejected. The four Coastway/email-booked containers and the early Meridane one went at 4.0°C and passed. The carrier's units held the 7.0°C setpoint within 0.4°C, so the carrier did what it was told. Fungicide stock does not track the outcome: K3 used the old stock and failed, and K5 and K7 used Pellacor and passed. Lower Serra fruit looked worse within failed containers, but that is not shown to be the cause. Next steps: correct the product record now. One container is at sea and one is queued for 10 Oct, so have Meridane reset both to 4°C. Add a check of reefer settings against the product specification before each submission. Hold off on the cargo claim, the Lower Serra suspension and the supplier reversal. Confidence is high. Extra loggers are optional.

The departures are concentrated in one place: 8 of the 11 associates on the Kestrel matter resigned, against 1 of 13 who were never on it. All 11 Kestrel associates report to the same new partner, Dorian Faulk, and he supervises no one else. Pay is the same across the group, and the billable-target change applied to every group. Neither explains why only Kestrel staff are leaving. So I doubt the retention payment would fix the problem, and announcing it and closing the review would be a mistake.

What I can't tell is whether the cause is the workload (months of weekends on document review) or Faulk's supervision (late-night corrections copied to the whole team). On the records, the two can't be separated. Survey comments point to both. I only collected one piece of evidence, so my confidence on that point is low.

Next step: commission the confidential external interviews, about £9k and three weeks. Ask questions that separate supervision from workload. Then pick the fix, which may be contract reviewers, a change of supervisor, or both. Also start tracking matter and supervising partner in attrition reports.

The rejects come from an interaction. Arnholt resin arrives wetter (0.27–0.33% at the dryer inlet) than Quillan (0.11–0.14%). Dryer D5 is degraded, with a dew point of about −16 to −19 °C against −40 °C. D5 can still dry Quillan acceptably, but it cannot dry Arnholt to the 0.20% limit.

- Arnholt in D5 on Press 5 had about 10% rejects.
- Arnholt on Press 7, whose dryer D7 is healthy, had 0.8%.
- Quillan in D5 had 0.9%.
- Arnholt lot A-2291 dried in a −40 °C portable dryer and fed to Press 5 gave 0.8% rejects, against 10.4% through D5 the day before.

The new operators are not the cause. Their reject rate matches the experienced operators' on both resins. The second shift looks worse only because all its VX runs on Press 5. Do not put them on performance plans.

This week, repair D5 and restore its original alarm limit. Keep Arnholt off D5 until D5 is verified at −40 °C. Add a moisture check at the press feed throat for every resin lot. Routing Arnholt to Press 7 alone would stop the rejects but leave D5 broken.

One gap remains. Arnholt was stored in the north annex and Quillan in the main warehouse, so storage and supplier are confounded. Ask Arnholt for the wetness at shipment, and hold off on moving the octabins until that is known.

Cancelling RotaWeave would not fix this. The drop is concentrated at Dock Street and Westgate, which have both the app and no coordinator since 1 May. Millbrook has the app but kept its coordinator, and its numbers are stable. Quarry Lane lost its coordinator but never went live on the app, and it is also stable. The mechanism is clear. The basic app tier has no recurring bookings, so regulars keep their usual slot only if staff book it before each Thursday release. Staff did that about 74 times a week before May and about 3 a week since. Of the April regulars at the two sites, 129 lost their usual slot, and 88% of them are now inactive. Among callbacks, 44 of 61 said nobody booked them. Background-check renewal and Commonplate don't explain it: 121 of the 123 who lapsed held a current check. Low satisfaction is a symptom, not the cause. Next steps: use the unused admin seat to book regulars into their usual slots at Dock Street and Westgate, phone lapsed volunteers to offer their slot back, and review after 60 days. Don't suspend checks, drop inactive people from the figures, or pay $14k to cancel. I'm fairly confident, but the site comparison covers only three sites, so treat the interaction conclusion as strong but not certain.

Regular volunteers are leaving because of two changes that only cause harm together. Regulars then lost their usual slots, mostly to new or corporate sign-ups. 88% of those who lost a slot at least twice are now inactive, against 11% of those who kept theirs. Millbrook has the app and a coordinator, and holds steady. Quarry Lane lost its coordinator but has no app, and also holds steady. Background checks are not the cause: 121 of the 123 who lapsed had a current check. Commonplate is not the cause either: only 2 of the 61 people reached by phone had joined another group. Cancelling RotaWeave would not address this and costs $14,000. Instead, assign someone to book regulars into their usual slots at Dock Street and Westgate, and phone lapsed volunteers to offer their old slots back. Check the results after 60 days. Do not suspend the checks or drop inactive names from the roster. Confidence is high. The evidence comes from two sites and a partial callback sample.

The Android login drop is almost certainly caused by a new Corvane edge rule, not release 6.14. Corvane's 3 March rule-pack update added a rule (AUTO-LIB-17). It blocks password-login requests from the nettle-http library when they carry no edge session cookie. The Android app uses that library for every API call. The rule started blocking at 10:41 UTC, and the added failures are HTTP 403 rejections that began that same minute on every app version, including 6.11 and older. Failure rates were the same for phones with and without the March security patch. Quick-unlock is unaffected. About 41,000 blocked installs, 92% of which had logged in successfully in the previous 90 days, look like real customers rather than bots. So I would not roll back 6.14. I would also not raise bot sensitivity or exclude blocked attempts from the KPI, since both would worsen the problem or hide it. Next step: ask Corvane to set the 3 March rules to log-only on the mobile password path, keeping the other protections on. Then confirm in telemetry that Android password success returns to about 96%. I'm confident in the cause. The link between the drop and the extra calls is plausible but not proven, because call reason codes are unreliable.

First-contact resolution fell because of the 14 April Finance change. It cut the credit an agent can apply on a call from £100 to £25 and automatically refers larger cases to the Billing Resolution team. The share of billing calls referred rose from 7% to 54% that same week. Referred calls resolve only about a third of the time, against 82% for the rest, and customers then call back to ask for status. This matches the timing and the size of the drop. The new starters are not the cause. Their referral rate and tenure-level results match the experienced agents, and experienced agents' resolution fell by the same amount. The IVR change came two weeks after the drop, and tariff calls still resolve at 85%. Workload is not tested, so I'm unsure about it. I'm fairly confident (about 85%) in the Finance-change explanation. Don't put the April starters on performance plans, and don't pause the IVR work on this basis. Agree a revised credit limit with Finance, with post-call sampling of credits, and trial it on two teams for six weeks. Track resolution and the rate of unsupported credits before rolling out wider. Finance has said it would consider this if unsupported credits stay under 1% of value. A multi-month dashboard rebuild can wait, since MI can rerun the breakdown for chosen teams within a day.

The enrolment drop is mainly a pricing effect, not an Admissions Office failure. Applications, admits and GPA all rose, so the applicant pool was not the problem. Yield fell by about the same amount for early-action admits (45.2% to 37.8%), whose decisions came out on time on the old system, as for regular-decision admits (39.0% to 31.5%), whose decisions were late. Slow turnaround therefore doesn't explain the fall. By scholarship tier, yield fell sharply only where award amounts were cut. Dean's yield went from 45.2% to 31.9% and Merit from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential awards were unchanged and yield stayed flat at about 36%. No-award yield also stayed roughly flat (38.5% to 37.0%). The Board's October 2025 schedule change relied on an old elasticity estimate. I'm fairly confident, though the tier data doesn't split early action from regular decision, and I didn't check the missing-transcript claims or the reader-staffing effect. Don't replace the director on this basis. Take a proposal to the finance committee to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, with the revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Also set a turnaround target for regular decision, since late answers are still a service problem. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the transcript issue is verified.

Don't roll back the gateway. The latency jump came from the storage compaction tuning change pushed fleet-wide at about 23:40 on 2 Nov, not from gateway 5.8. Regional gateway arrival times were staggered over six hours. Latency jumped in every cell within minutes of the config push, and the cells that hadn't yet received 5.8 jumped too. One cell, aps-3, got 5.8 but skipped the config push, and its latency stayed at about 94 ms. Rolling euw-1 back to 5.7 changed nothing. After the push, compaction threads went from 2 to 6, disk use went to 97%, and disk read waits rose from 9 to 205 ms. A fleet-wide rollback would remove the security fix, which is due by 30 Nov, and wouldn't fix latency. Network and traffic growth don't explain the timing. Next step: revert the compaction change in one cell first, e.g. use-1. Watch p99 and compaction backlog, then extend the revert. Don't pause compaction, because backlog would reach the 15% danger point. Hold off on throttling Orrin until the backlog attribution report due 10 Nov. Confidence is high. The main unknown is what drove the backlog growth.

Store 14's shrink rise is not yet proven to be real. The figures are interim estimates from partial cycle counts, with an error margin of about ±0.6 points per quarter. Across the chain, about half of the two-quarter rises of this size were not confirmed by the year-end full count. Store 14's full-count shrink was 1.5–1.8% in the past three years. The recorded shoplifting increase is unreliable as a signal, because the incident app launched chain-wide on 1 April and recorded incidents rose across the chain while chain shrink stayed flat. The ethics-line tip was checked against CCTV and not substantiated. The sales mix did not change, so it does not explain the rise. Nothing yet separates self-checkout, customer theft and staff theft as causes, and the evidence doesn't isolate any of them. I am fairly confident in this, not certain. Next: keep store 14 in the 7 December full count and do not drop it. Hold off on a guard, on pulling or staffing the lanes, and on any action against the stocker until the count result is compared with the interim figures. Doubling cycle counts adds little. If the count confirms the rise, investigate by product category and compare with the neighbouring stores.

The most likely cause is contaminated brake fluid, not driver technique or the new pads. All 11 Eastgate vans with soft-pedal complaints were serviced at Northfield Motor Services while the in-house bay was closed. Northfield used an old bulk drum with a missing cap that had taken on water. Two vans that got fluid from a fresh sealed drum had no complaints. Two vans (LK-217, LK-224) tested at 149–152°C boiling point, against 255°C for sealed stock. Renewing their fluid is recorded in the Northfield warranty card. Northfield recommended rechecking the other vans on 25 Sep, and nobody replied. The same drivers had no problems in other vans on the same hilly routes. Calder Road vans fitted with the same Tessaro pads show no complaints. I'm fairly sure of this, though I haven't tested the other 11 vans' fluid directly. Next steps: take all 13 Northfield-serviced vans off the road until their fluid is tested and renewed from sealed stock. Check Calder Road's fluid source too. Do not discipline drivers, because they reported a real safety fault. Hold off on changing pad supplier until there is evidence about the pads.

The evidence points away from the agency operators and the printer firmware. Printer job records show every Veltranol job from 2 Jun to 3 Oct carried a 24-month shelf life and printed correctly. Other products are unconfirmed. Keep the camera check on. Confidence is fairly high.

Analyzer B looks fine. One Level 2 potassium QC result failed. The repeat from the same vial passed. The other two levels in that run were normal. There were no other QC rule violations in a month, and the means before and after the lot change are the same. That fits the expected rate of chance flags (about one or two a month). QC also ran on schedule, so skipped QC from short staffing is not supported. Re-testing 43 samples on Analyzer A agreed with Analyzer B within 0.02 mmol/L on average. The patient moving median was normal.

The Ward 6 highs are not an analyzer problem. They split evenly between Analyzer A and Analyzer B. Most of them had long transit times because the tube station is down. Four renal overflow patients also arrived. That is a confound, so the transit delay is a likely contributor but not proven.

What to sign off:
- Return Analyzer B potassium to service and close the review with no amendments.
- Do not recall about 2,900 results, quarantine the lot, or widen the limits to ±4 SD. Widening would blind QC.
- Optionally add extra Level 2 QC for a week.
- Do not record "sampling disturbance" as confirmed. It can't be distinguished from chance.
- Ask Ward 6 to send repeat samples, and get the tube station fixed.

I'm fairly confident, but I did not collect any further evidence.

The rise in cancellations is mainly a Quillbook connector problem, not a pricing problem. Quillbook retired an old invoice interface on 30 March. Since then the connector has silently dropped or duplicated invoices. 58,300 invoices were affected across 1,212 accounts, and 34% of those accounts had cancelled by 31 July, against 8% of the Quillbook accounts with no recorded failure. Among accounts with no connector, churn is flat at about 1.9%, whether or not the price rose. Founders accounts, whose price did not change, churn as much as repriced ones on Quillbook. The seat-size pattern in the finance analysis is explained by larger accounts being more likely to use Quillbook. The failures were logged as warnings, so the health panel missed them.

Recommendation for the board: make the Quillbook v3 fix the top engineering priority, since it is a three to four week job. Contact every Quillbook account, including those that cancelled, to correct their invoices. Keep the duplicate-invoice hold on, because it protects customers' books. Don't reverse the price now, and hold off on the Tallymarsh rebuild. Review the Tallymarsh log first, because the evidence so far shows only small numbers. I'm fairly confident in this. The main gap is that the Tallymarsh log hasn't been reviewed.

The gap is mostly a tenure effect, not a location effect. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so most remote staff are new: only 32% of remote staff have the 18 months in level the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28.2% vs 28.6%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and promotion rates (20.0% vs 21.1%) are nearly the same. Applying office rates to the remote tenure mix predicts 8.2%, close to the 7.6% observed. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% vs 11.6%), and job mix doesn't explain it. Caveat: only 110 remote staff are eligible, so a real gap of a few points can't be ruled out. Manager comments hint at informal favouritism in who gets urgent work, but that isn't measured. Don't confirm proximity bias or announce the three-day office rule. It would penalise about 180 people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Instead, pause it, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, track stretch-work allocation, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Confidence: fairly high.

The crash gap is mostly not caused by the Tiled Canvas flag. Everyone who can get the flag is on build 7.4.0, and 7.4.0 was already crashing at about 2% on 2–3 Sep, before the flag ramp began. 7.3.2 stays near 0.7%. Within 7.4.0, flagged users crash 2.10% versus 1.98% for the random holdout. That 0.12-point difference is within noise (interval −0.08 to +0.32). Device mix, usage and the sync-service deploy don't explain it: they're similar across groups, and 7.3.2 was flat after 9 Sep. The top 7.4.0 crash is a native crash in the upgraded image library (Pixelda, HEIF decoding), 41% of events. The app-store console, which is independent of the crash SDK, shows the same gap, so it's not a reporting artifact. A small flag effect can't be ruled out. Turning the flag off and releasing 7.4.0 to 100% would ship the real problem and call the incident closed. Next steps: hold 7.4.0 at 25%, fix the Pixelda crashes, and keep the flag as is. Widening the holdout would measure any flag effect faster, and the rework of tile memory can wait for that result. Confidence is fairly high.

Since the night receiving team was cut from six to four (27 July), the median time from unloading to reaching a cold chamber rose from about 44 minutes to nearly 4 hours. Pallets wait in an unrefrigerated dock area at 15–17°C. Night-shift write-off rates rose from 0.6% to 2.9% for every supplier, while day-shift rates stayed flat. Trailer data that can't be edited shows Haverlow loads were 2.4–3.5°C when the doors opened and were empty by about 23:30. The warm receipt probe readings of 6.5–8°C were logged hours later, at confirmation. The chambers held temperature. A chargeback and volume shift against Haverlow would punish the wrong party and rest on misleading readings. I'm fairly confident in this. Next steps: restore the night team to six, cap dock-to-chamber time and monitor it weekly from scan data, and hold the chargeback. Keep the receiving probe. Separately, ask Corriebank for claim-level data. The rise in their credits coincides with self-certification, but that link is not shown, and some of the credits may be for genuinely warmed product.

The rise in chilled write-offs is mostly an internal problem, not a Haverlow problem. The dock is unrefrigerated and ran 15–17°C overnight. Night-received lots now have a 2.9% write-off rate, up from 0.6%, and this holds for every supplier. Day-shift rates are flat. Haverlow's trailer records show product at 2.4–3.5°C when the doors opened, with no trend. The chambers held temperature. So the warm receiving probe readings reflect product that had already warmed on the dock. They do not show warm product arriving. I'm quite sure of this. A chargeback and a volume shift would punish the wrong party. Dropping the night probe would hide the problem. Lead with restoring night receiving to six and setting a maximum dock-to-chamber time, tracked weekly. Separately, reconcile a sample of Corriebank's claims. The rise in delayed alarm responses comes mainly from the 12 August alarm relay server move, not from agency staff. The "like-for-like" refresh imported only 3 of 14 forwarding rules. The lost rules included the 15-second hold-off for brief SpO2 dips, suppression of repeat notifications, and routing of technical alarms to the charge phone only. Phone notifications per nurse in Pods A–C roughly doubled, from about 38 to about 82 per shift. Acknowledgement time doubled from 34 s to 71 s. Pod D was still on the old server and shows no change in notifications or incidents. Pod D has a similar agency share, which counts against the staffing explanation. Alarms arriving at the relay from the monitors were flat (about 95 per patient-day), which counters the acuity and monitor-update explanations. Core, agency and new-graduate nurses all show similar incident rates in Pods A–C, so the problem is the system rather than individuals. I'm quite confident (about 85–90%). Sick leave may be partly driven by alarm load, but that is unproven, and the virus season is a rival explanation. Recommended: restore and validate the old rules, then track notifications per nurse and acknowledgement times weekly. Don't cap agency use or open performance reviews, and don't switch off phone forwarding for SpO2 and technical alarms. Wireless coverage is unlikely to be the cause, though one detail is unresolved: the relay logs record dispatch to the phone system, not receipt by a handset, so the Room 14 reports of phones not ringing remain unchecked.

The rejections trace to the cooperative's own paperwork. When Meridane bookings moved to the new documentation suite, the mandarin product record was copied from the avocado record. It carried a 7.0°C carriage temperature instead of the 4.0°C specification. Every Meridane container since go-live (K3, K4, K6, K8, K9) was sent at 7.0°C and the units held that setpoint. All five were rejected. Every container at 4.0°C passed, including Pellacor-treated fruit on Coastway (K5, K7) and old-stock fungicide K3 at 7°C, which failed. So the fungicide, the carrier's equipment and the routing are not the explanation. Lower Serra fruit did show more decay inside rejected containers, but that is only an association and it is not a reason to suspend growers. Next steps: correct the mandarin product record to 4.0°C now. Have Meridane reset the container at sea (sailed 3 Oct) and the one queued for 10 Oct. Add a check that compares reefer settings with the product specification before submission. Do not file the cargo claim, suspend growers, switch fungicide back or penalise the contractor on current evidence. Independent loggers are a reasonable extra safeguard. Confidence is high. The remaining uncertainty is whether Lower Serra fruit has any separate effect.

The rising rejects are not caused by the new operators, and not by Arnholt resin alone. They come from a combination. Arnholt resin arrives wetter, probably because it sits in the north annex. Dryer D5 has degraded, and its alarm limit was loosened in week 31. D5 can't dry the wetter resin enough, and Press 5 then makes parts that crack and splay. The evidence for this:
- Press 5 on Arnholt rejects about 10%. Press 5 on Quillan rejects 0.9%. Press 7 on Arnholt rejects 0.8%.
- Rejects are the same across shifts and the same for new and experienced operators.
- Arnholt lot A-2291 gave 0.8% rejects when dried in a good dryer and 10.4% through D5.
I'm quite confident in this. The one open question is whether the annex storage is what makes Arnholt wet. Storage and supplier are confounded in the samples.
This week:
1. Don't put the six operators on improvement plans.
2. Keep Arnholt off Press 5 now by routing it to Press 7 or a verified dryer.
3. Repair D5 (heater and desiccant) and confirm it reads −40 °C.
4. Restore the original alarm limit.
5. Check moisture at the press feed throat for every resin lot.
6. Hold off on renting space or dropping Arnholt until you've tested conditioned storage.

The rejects come from an interaction. Arnholt resin arrives wetter than Quillan. Dryer D5 has degraded, with dew point around −16 to −19 °C against −40 °C, and its alarm limit was loosened in week 31. Together they leave resin at the Press 5 throat at 0.25–0.31% moisture against a 0.20% limit. That gives splay and latch cracks. Press 5 with Arnholt rejects about 10%. Press 5 with Quillan rejects 0.9%. Press 7, which has a good dryer, rejects about 0.8% with either supplier. Arnholt dried in a good portable dryer and run on Press 5 rejected 0.8%. The second-shift gap exists because Press 5 is the only press that runs VX on second shift. New and experienced operators reject at the same rate on each resin, so do not discipline the new operators. Dropping Arnholt is not warranted. The trial missed this because it ran on Press 7 only. I'm quite sure of this. The one open point is whether storing Arnholt in the north annex explains its wetter inlet resin. Annex storage and supplier are confounded in the samples. Next steps: repair D5 and its heater, change the desiccant, and restore the −40 alarm limit. Keep Arnholt off D5 until the dew point is verified. Add a throat moisture check for every lot. Test annex storage separately before paying to move stock.

The volunteer drop is not mainly about the app itself, the background checks, or Commonplate. It comes from two changes acting together. RotaWeave's basic tier keeps no standing weekly slots. A regular keeps a slot only if staff book it before the Thursday release. Until 1 May, coordinators did that booking. At Dock Street and Westgate the coordinator posts were cut that day, and bookings on behalf of volunteers fell from 74 a week to 3. About 129 of 213 regulars lost their usual slot at least twice, and 88% of them are now inactive, against 11% of those who kept it. Millbrook has the app and a coordinator, and its numbers are stable. Quarry Lane lost its coordinator but has no app and a paper roster, and it is also stable. The background-check deadline hit all sites equally, and 21 of the 23 deactivated volunteers came back. 121 of the 123 who lapsed had a current check, so renewal isn't the cause. Only 2 of the 61 people reached by callback said they had joined another group. Don't cancel RotaWeave, suspend the checks or purge the rolls. Instead, assign someone to book regulars into their usual slots before each release at Dock Street and Westgate, and phone lapsed volunteers to offer their slot back. I'm fairly confident in this. The main gap is that the evidence is observational.

Instead, assign someone to book regulars into their usual slots at Dock Street and Westgate, call lapsed volunteers to offer their old slot back, and review the results after 60 days. Plan for Quarry Lane before its 6 October go-live, because it has the same gap.

The Android login drop is almost certainly caused by a vendor rule, not by release 6.14. On 3 March at 10:38 UTC, Corvane's rule-pack update added a rule (AUTO-LIB-17) that blocks password requests from Android's networking library. Blocks began at 10:41, and the added failures are all HTTP 403 rejections. They hit every app version, every Android OS version and phones with or without the security patch alike. Quick-unlock, iOS and web are untouched. About 92% of the blocked installs had logged in successfully before, so these are real customers, not bots. Rolling back 6.14 would not help, since 6.14 is only 5–10% of traffic and its success rate matches the others. Screen redesign, OS patch and auth-token change are not supported. The call-volume rise is likely partly fee notices, so that link is unproven. Next: ask Corvane to set the new rule to log-only on the mobile password path, keeping other protections, and confirm in telemetry that password success recovers. Don't raise bot sensitivity or exclude blocked attempts from the KPI; that would worsen lockouts and hide the problem. Continue the rollout while tracking by version. Confidence is high.

The Android login drop is almost certainly caused by a new vendor rule, not by release 6.14. Corvane's 3 March rule-pack update added a rule that blocks any request from the nettle-http library on the password-login path when it has no edge session cookie. The Android app uses that library for every API call. Blocks began at 10:41 UTC, three minutes after the rule activated. They hit about 41,300 installs, 92% of which had logged in successfully before, so these are mostly real customers. Every Android version failed at the same moment, including old versions that didn't get 6.14. Quick-unlock, iOS and web were untouched. The failures are all HTTP 403 on password submissions, so credential-stuffing, the OS patch, the new password screen and the auth-token change don't explain them. Next step: ask Corvane to switch only that rule to log-only on the mobile password path, keeping rate limits, lockout and other rules on, then confirm in telemetry that Android password success returns to about 96%. Don't roll back 6.14, raise bot sensitivity, or drop blocked attempts from the KPI. Raising sensitivity would block more customers, and the KPI change would hide the problem. My confidence is high. The remaining gap is whether 6.14 has any smaller separate issue.

FCR fell because of the 14 April Finance change, not the new starters. It cut the credit an agent can apply on a call from £100 to £25 and sends anything larger to the Billing Resolution team. Billing calls referred there rose from 7% to 54% overnight that week. Referred calls resolve at about 34%, against 82% for the rest, and that matches the site-wide drop. The referral rate is the same for new and tenured agents (56%, 54% and 53%), and tenured agents fell about 8 points too. So the April intake is not the cause. The tariff increase shifted the call mix, but tariff calls resolve well. I did not check the IVR or workload explanations directly. They look minor, but they are not fully ruled out. I'm fairly confident in this diagnosis. Don't start performance plans. They would punish the wrong group. Agree a revised credit limit with Finance and trial it on two teams for six weeks. Use post-call sampling and track FCR and unsupported credits. Hold off on a site-wide restore until the trial reports. Also ask Management Information to produce the breakdown by referral status for the trial teams. It can do this within a day.

The evidence points to the cut in merit awards, not the Admissions Office, as the main cause of the drop. Yield fell only in the Dean's tier (45.2% to 31.9%) and the Merit tier (44.9% to 32.3%), where awards were cut from $14,000 to $9,000 and from $9,000 to $5,000. It was flat in the Presidential tier, where awards were unchanged, and nearly flat among students with no merit award. Applications, admits and GPA all rose, so a weaker applicant pool is not the explanation. Early-action students had their decisions on the old timetable and old system. Their yield still fell by about the same amount (45.2% to 37.8%) as regular decision (39.0% to 31.5%). So the late regular-decision answers were not the main driver, though they did hurt some individual students. Regular decision was probably a smaller contributor, and I can't size it. I'm fairly confident, but this is not a controlled test. Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take a proposal to the finance committee to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, with the revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Also set a monthly turnaround target for regular decision. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the missing-transcript claims are checked.

The latency regression is almost certainly caused by the 2 Nov storage compaction tuning change, not gateway 5.8. That change raised compaction threads from 2 to 6. Disks went from 41% to 97% utilised within minutes of the push, and node-side GET time rose from 61 ms to 262 ms. In every cell, p99 jumped within minutes of the push, regardless of when 5.8 arrived. One cell, aps-3, got 5.8 but skipped the push, and its p99 stayed at about 94 ms. Rolling euw-1 back to 5.7 changed nothing. Network and traffic growth don't fit the timing.

Do not roll back the gateway. It would not fix latency and would reopen the signature vulnerability, which audit requires closed by 30 Nov. Do not pause compaction fleet-wide: backlog would grow and disks would fill.

Next: revert the tuning in one cell first, watch p99 and backlog, then extend it to the others. Consider Orrin pacing later. The backlog is not yet attributed, and the projection shows no breach of 15% before 13 Nov. Confidence is high on the main cause, and moderate on backlog sources.

The gateway 5.8 release is not the cause. The slowdown came from the storage compaction tuning change pushed the evening of 2 Nov. It raised compaction threads from 2 to 6. Disk use jumped from 41% to 97% within minutes of the push, and disk read waits went from 9 ms to 205 ms. In every cell the slowdown began within minutes of that push, regardless of when 5.8 arrived. One cell (aps-3) got 5.8 but skipped the push because of a change freeze. Its latency stayed at about 94 ms. Rolling back 5.8 in one cell (euw-1) changed nothing. The network shows no problem. Traffic growth is too small to explain it. I'm fairly confident (about 90%). What remains unknown is which source drove the earlier backlog growth: Orrin Media's migration or the lifecycle-expiry sweep. That attribution is due 10 Nov. Next steps: do not roll back the gateway, because it would reopen the security hole and fix nothing. Revert the compaction change in one cell first and watch p99 and backlog, then extend it to the rest. Do not pause compaction. Hold the Orrin rate limit until the attribution is in. Profile 5.8's CPU use later as routine work.

Across past store-years, about half of "two consecutive rises" patterns were not confirmed by the year-end full count. Store 14's own full-count shrink has stayed at 1.5–1.8% for three years. The rise is spread evenly across all departments, and sales mix has not changed. That fits measurement noise more than a shift in mix. The rise does not clearly point to self-checkout or customer theft. The shoplifting log counts went up chain-wide when the incident app launched, so they aren't a reliable signal. The ethics tip was checked against CCTV and showed routine cardboard bale runs, so there is no basis to discipline the stocker. Neighbouring stores show no matching trend, but that doesn't settle the cause.

Next steps: keep store 14 in the 7 December full count, and don't confirm Operations' request to drop it. Hold off on a guard, pulling the lanes, or any personnel action until the count result is compared with the interim figures. I am moderately sure. I did not collect any evidence that could directly test the self-checkout or customer-theft explanations.

Last week's 5xx rate (0.41%) is within the normal range for this service. Over the preceding 26 weeks the mean was 0.354% and the upper edge of the normal band was 0.482%. Earlier weeks reached 0.51%, 0.47% and 0.45%, and every one of those was investigated with no fault found. The burn-rate page did not fire (0.82x against a 2x threshold). The dashboard count matches the raw logs. The apparent "new pods error twice as often" result is a rollout warm-up effect. New pods start with an empty cache and time out against the database. The same gap appears in all five recent rollouts, including a config-only redeploy, and it adds only 10–20 errors. Bookings were unchanged and there were no customer complaints. I don't think v4.18 or the replica move is shown to be at fault. I'm fairly confident, but I haven't ruled out a small real effect from the release, the replica move or partner-sync traffic. Recommended: don't roll back and don't move the replica. Do not mute the alerting, because that would remove the safeguard. Note the week at ops review and apply the standard check to the week of 2 Nov. If that week goes above 0.48%, investigate it as an incident.

The Kestria buffering problem is almost certainly caused by the smart-TV app 5.2 release, not the new CDN. Rebuffering jumped on 9 Oct, when the app went live. The jump was in the same window as the cutover, which is why the CDN looked guilty. Session data shows smart-TV 5.2 at about 5.9% rebuffering on every ISP. Every other client, including web and mobile, runs at about 0.6–0.7% on the same Tessaline CDN and the same ISPs. The handball launch came two days after the jump, and match nights show no extra spike. So neither it nor ISP congestion explains the rise. I'm fairly confident, though I haven't seen the app's configuration record to name the exact setting. Do not send the breach notice, withhold fees or switch back to Corvane. That would punish the wrong party and leave the fault in place. Do not mute the alert either. Instead, roll Kestria's smart-TV app back to the 5.1 streaming settings and hold the wider 5.2 rollout until it is fixed. Then add app version and device breakdowns to the dashboard. The link between buffering and the October cancellations is unproven. Exit survey options had no quality choice, and the 1 Oct price rise is a competing cause. Hold off on a win-back offer until that is checked.

Don't send the breach notice. The rise in lost bags comes from the tag stock, not the handler. Since 1 September, Corvane tags printed on the new Fennick stock fail automatic reading about 11.8% of the time, against about 1.5% on the old stock. Corvane transfer tags and Pelion tags are unchanged at about 1.3%, so the baggage readers are working. Those failed bags go to the manual encode desk. Encode delays rose from 7 to 33 minutes, and 91% of the affected bags reach the lateral after it closes. Pelion has the same handler and the same crews, and its rate did not move. Corvane bags that read automatically are as reliable as before. On 14–16 October, counters that used old stock from stores had a 1.6% failure rate, while kiosks on new stock stayed at 12%. I'm fairly confident, about 85%. What we don't know is whether the cause is the stock itself or the printer heat settings the new stock needs. Next steps: put counters and kiosks back on Brackwater stock now, since it's under contract and in stores, and watch the read rate. Test the Fennick stock separately, including the printer settings. Hold off on any defect claim against Fennick until that test is done. A temporary extra encode workstation is a reasonable stopgap.

I can't tell yet whether the stock is defective or the printers need different heat settings. Do not send the breach notice or withhold the fee: the evidence points away from Tessaly. Return counters and kiosks to the Brackwater stock held in stores (about five weeks' supply). Then test the Fennick stock with printer settings. Hold any defect claim against Fennick until that test is done. Asking HBAA for an extra encode workstation in the evening is a reasonable stopgap. Confidence is about 80%.

The likely cause is contaminated brake fluid, not driver technique, the pads or the hills. Northfield Motor Services refilled 13 Eastgate vans with fluid from a bulk drum that had been open since March and had lost its cap. Two vans that came back on warranty tested at about 150°C boiling point, against 255°C for sealed stock. Those drums were opened 10 Sep or later for only LK-214 and LK-227. Those two vans have no complaints. The other 11 Northfield vans account for all 27 Eastgate complaints. Calder Road vans, which had the same pads and the same hills, have none. The 19 complaining drivers had no brake problems in non-Northfield vans, including 141 days on Upper Wend. Warning drivers would punish people who correctly reported a real fault, so don't do it. Next steps: pull every Northfield-serviced van from the bay closure out of service now. Test the fluid and renew it from sealed stock. Keep LK-209 parked until that is done. Ask Northfield for the full list of vans and which drum each came from. Pad switching can wait. The squeal rise is confounded by freshly fitted pads. I'm fairly confident, but I haven't tested the fluid in the vans that haven't been rechecked.

Floors 6-8 room comfort fell from 8.4 to 6.1, and their overall score fell from 8.6 to 7.4. The score recovered to 8.4 once cooling returned. Floors 1-5 were flat within normal variation. Cleanliness scores, inspection pass rates and kiosk metrics barely moved, so the housekeeping contractor and kiosks are not the problem. The survey method was unchanged. Don't give notice to Orrin, don't pull the kiosks, and don't drop the floor 6-8 responses from the reported score. That would hide a real failure. Do restore the deferred maintenance on both chillers, stock critical spares, and write a recovery protocol for cooling outages. Guests were already sent apologies and half-night credits. A return-stay offer is optional on top of that. The rate rise may have nudged the value score, but it is confounded with the usual August seasonal dip. Review that separately and don't reverse the rate yet. I'm fairly confident, and more evidence is unlikely to change these recommendations.
