The evidence points to a single chance QC flag, not a fault with the analyzer or the new reagent lot. The repeat of the same QC material passed. The other QC levels and sodium and chloride were fine. Level 2 averages are unchanged since the lot change. All QC ran on schedule, so skipped QC is not supported. Patient samples re-run on Analyzer A agreed within 0.02 mmol/L on average, and the patient median is stable. This kind of flag is expected roughly once or twice a month. The Ward 6 high potassiums are split evenly between Analyzers A and B. They coincide with the tube outage, with longer transit times, and with four overflow renal patients. Delay in transit is plausible, but the other explanations aren't ruled out. No repeat samples have been requested. I am fairly confident (about 70-80%). I did not collect further evidence. What to sign off: return Analyzer B potassium to service. Close the 186-result review with no amendments. Don't recall about 2,900 results, quarantine the lot or widen the limits. Consider an extra Level 2 QC per shift for a week. Do not record a sampling glitch as the confirmed cause, because it can't be shown. Ask Ward 6 for repeat samples, and push for the tube repair.

Analyzer B most likely had one chance QC outlier or a brief sampling glitch. The evidence does not show a real fault. The repeat passed within 21 minutes. Sodium and chloride were fine. Level 2 means were unchanged after the lot change (5.81 before, 5.80 after). QC ran on schedule, so the staffing theory isn't supported. Patient samples re-run on Analyzer A agreed with B (mean difference +0.02, limit 0.20). The patient median is stable. I can't tell which of the two explanations is right, so I wouldn't record either as confirmed.

Ward 6's high potassiums split evenly between the two analyzers (7 each). The ward's high-result rate is up, and the tube outage means long transport delays. Four renal overflow patients also arrived. Delay is the more likely explanation, though it's an association rather than proven.

What to sign off: return Analyzer B to potassium service and close the 186-result review with no amendments. Don't recall results, quarantine the lot or widen the limits. Add extra Level 2 QC at the start of each shift for a week. Ask Ward 6 for repeat samples on current high results, and push for the tube repair. I'm moderately confident. I did not collect any further evidence.

The rise in VA-220 failures is almost certainly a Pellacott valve problem, not an installer or firmware one. Brenmoor's lab matched claims to installer and firmware. Pellacott 2026 valves fail at about 40 per 1,000 whichever installer or firmware version is involved. Durrant-Hale valves stay at 5–7 per 1,000 in every group. Unused Pellacott 2026 warehouse valves leak at the seat 11% of the time, against 1% for 2025-built and 0% for Durrant-Hale. Pellacott's leak-test rig was out of service from 9 Jan 2026, and no VA-220 test program was loaded on the other rigs. Its 2026 certificates repeat four fixed sequences of values, some already used in Nov 2025. So the certificates very likely do not reflect real tests. That also explains the score rise: the 'test-record' component went from 58 to 100 on paperwork alone. The seal and line change is a plausible physical cause, but it can't be separated from the line move, so it is not proven. Next steps: do not release the six held lots on new certificates. Quarantine 2026-built Pellacott stock, suspend dock-to-stock, and retest with helium in-house. Press Pellacott for rig logs. Drop the installer remediation and chargeback plan. Check other suppliers' records separately. I'm fairly confident, though the root cause of the seal failure is still open.

Drop the installer remediation plan and chargebacks. Fix the scoring so it needs rig logs or witnessed tests. Check other suppliers' records. The Corlin seal and Line 3 effects cannot yet be separated, so don't mandate a seal change yet. I'm fairly confident in this.

Reinstate the 47 cases, have Corvane's team and Halvard verify containment on each, and remove the integration account's category-edit rights. Also review the 96-case queue. Ask Brackwater for a written explanation and keep the service credits in reserve until the contract is checked. I'm fairly confident in the main finding, less so on intent and on the rules question.

The rise in cancellations is mostly not a pricing problem. It comes from the Quillbook accounting connector. Quillbook retired its old invoice interface on 30 March. Since then the connector has silently dropped or duplicated invoices: 58,300 across 1,212 accounts. Of those accounts, 34% have cancelled, against 8% of Quillbook accounts with no recorded failure. Quillbook accounts churn at about 6% a month whether they are repriced or on the locked price. Accounts with no connector, which are most of the base, are barely changed (1.9% against 1.8%), including the largest seat band. The earlier link between bigger price increases and more cancellations is explained by the fact that bigger accounts are more likely to use Quillbook. The failures are logged only as warnings, so the health panel misses them. The ticket is rated low severity and has no schedule.

What to do next:
- Make the Quillbook fix (move to the new interface) the top engineering priority.
- Contact every Quillbook account, including those that cancelled, to correct their invoices.
- Do not reverse the price rise.
- Do not switch off the duplicate-invoice hold. It has kept 3,870 duplicates out of customers' books.
- Hold the Tallymarsh rebuild until its log has been reviewed. Its churn change is within normal variation.

I'm fairly confident in this. Support slowness is a probable secondary factor, but I haven't established it.

The gap looks mostly like a difference in eligibility, not a bias against remote work. Only about a third of remote staff (32%) have the 18 months in their current level that the policy requires, against about 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination, approval and promotion rates are almost the same (20.0% remote vs 21.1% office). Matching the office rates to the remote tenure mix predicts 8.2% for remote staff, and the observed rate is 7.6%. That is a close fit. The eligible remote group is only 110 people, so a modest real difference can't be ruled out. The dashboard divides by all staff, so it mixes tenure with location. Requiring office days would not fix the main driver, would hit about 180 remote staff hired on home-based contracts, and has no support in this evidence. Don't confirm the proximity-bias diagnosis or announce the rule. Put it on hold. Report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check that at the FY2027 cycle. Separately, find out whether remote staff get fewer stretch assignments. The staffing data can't answer that, and the managers' comments hint at it. Also check why remote staff are newer, and whether more of them leave. I'm fairly confident in the main finding, less so on the smaller questions.

The gap looks mostly like a difference in time in role, not work location. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so most remote staff are new: 32% of them had the 18 months in level the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28% vs 29%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and overall promotion rates (20% vs 21%) are almost the same. The expected remote rate from this mix is 8.2%, against 7.6% observed. Remote staff don't leave more often, and the job-family explanation doesn't hold. One caveat: only 110 remote staff are eligible, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. Evidence on unequal access to high-profile work is anecdotal. Don't confirm proximity bias, and don't adopt the three-day office rule. It would penalise about 180 people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Next: hold the proposal. Change reporting to compare eligible people only, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Meanwhile, collect staffing data on who gets stretch assignments. Clear communication of the promotion criteria to remote staff is a cheap extra step.

The crash gap is mostly not caused by the Tiled Canvas flag. Everyone who can have the flag is on build 7.4.0, and that build crashes at about 2% from 2 Sep, before the flag ramp began. Build 7.3.2 stays at about 0.7%. Within 7.4.0, flag-on users crash only 0.12 points more than the random holdout, and that difference could be zero. Device mix and usage are similar across the groups. The sync-service deploy shows no effect on 7.3.2. The leading crash cluster, about 41% of events, is in the upgraded Pixelda image library decoding HEIF images, and it appears only in 7.4.0. The crash-reporting SDK change doesn't explain it, because the app store's own counts match. Don't turn the flag off and release 7.4.0 to everyone: that would ship the real problem to all users and leave the incident unresolved. Hold the rollout at 25%, and fix the Pixelda crashes first, for example by reverting the library or patching the HEIF decoding. Keep the existing holdout, and consider widening it, to settle whether the flag adds a small effect, which can't be ruled out yet. Confidence is fairly high on the build being the main driver and moderate on the flag's own effect.

Don't do the director's plan: it would ship the real crash to 100% of users and close the incident with the cause unfixed. Hold 7.4.0 at 25%, and fix or roll back the Pixelda upgrade. I'm fairly confident, with the small flag effect still unresolved.

Get an independent delay analysis that uses the platform's timestamps and the crane ledger, and have it separate out any genuine CO-09 delay. The evidence points mainly at Callerby's own decision. The tower crane and frame crew went to the Kestrel job from October 2025 until April, and the frame stood idle. The architect did not cause the delay. The independent RFI platform shows 62 of 64 queries answered within the contract period, with a median of 4 working days. The two late ones were minor and from May 2026. The claim's "late RFIs" mostly count time the drafts sat unsent at Callerby. The change orders are mostly small. CO-09 (£212k, MRI move, issued 6 Nov) is a real structural change. However, the crane had already left in October, and its connection query was answered in 4 days. Do not submit the claim as drafted. Its RFI figures are contradicted by the platform record, and submitting it risks credibility and exposure. Do not discipline the superintendent for answering a direct question honestly. Do not suspend the incentive scheme yet, because its role in the crane move is unproven. Commission an independent delay analysis, using the platform timestamps and the crane ledger. Use it to decide whether a narrow CO-09 claim or a negotiated settlement is justified. Review Fenmore's 6% fee incentive. Confidence is moderate. The CO-09 share of the delay is the main unknown.

The jump in chilled write-offs comes mainly from inside the DC, not from Haverlow. Haverlow's trailer sensors show product at 2.4–3.5°C when the doors open. The trailers were unloaded by about 23:00–23:40, but the receipt probe readings were keyed at 02:30–03:20. In between, pallets sat on an unrefrigerated dock at 15–17°C. Since the night receiving team went from six to four in week 31, night dock-to-chamber time rose from 44 minutes to almost 4 hours. The night write-off rate went from 0.6% to 2.9%, and it is the same for Haverlow, Pellridge and own-label. Day shift is unchanged. The chambers held temperature. So the warm "receiving temperatures" mostly reflect dock dwell, and a chargeback and volume move against Haverlow would punish the wrong party. Next: restore night receiving capacity, or otherwise get chilled pallets into the chambers quickly. Set a maximum dock-to-chamber time and track it weekly from scan data. Do not drop the probe. Separately, sample Corriebank's claims against lots and receiving shift before changing credit terms. The cause of the DC-stage rise is well established. How much of the credit rise is over-claiming is still open.

The rise in delayed alarm responses most likely comes from the 12 August relay server move. The import skipped 11 of 14 forwarding rules, including the 15-second hold-off, repeat-notification suppression and routing of technical alarms to the charge phone. The IT team's test and sign-off didn't catch it. Since then, phone notifications per nurse in Pods A-C have roughly doubled (about 38 to 80+ per shift). Acknowledgement time doubled, from 34 to 71 seconds. Incidents rose about fivefold for core, agency and new-graduate nurses alike. Pod D, still on the old server, saw no change, even though its agency share is similar. That rules out agency staffing, acuity and the monitor update as main causes. Bedside alarm volume was flat, and there was no step on 23-24 September. Sick leave rising with the alarm load is plausible but not proven. I'm fairly confident (about 85-90%). Don't cap agency use or open performance reviews. That would punish the wrong people. Don't switch off SpO2 phone forwarding either. Instead, restore the rules (about 4 hours plus clinical validation), get Clinical Engineering and the alarm committee to sign off, and track notifications per nurse and acknowledgement times weekly. Check the room 14 reports of phones not ringing separately. Wireless coverage is unconfirmed.

The rejections trace to a data error, not the fungicide, Lower Serra fruit, or the carrier. When Meridane bookings moved to the new documentation system on 4 Aug, the mandarin product record had been copied from avocados. It carried a 7.0°C carriage temperature instead of your 4.0°C specification. The system sent that to Meridane automatically. Meridane's units held 7°C as instructed. All five Meridane containers sent that way (K3, K4, K6, K8, K9) were rejected. Every container at 4°C passed, including Pellacor-treated Coastway loads (K5, K7). Meridane's own units therefore did not fail, and Pellacor did not fail either. K3 used old fungicide and was still rejected. Lower Serra pallets were worse inside the rejected containers, but there is no comparison in accepted containers, so treat that as unproven. Do next: correct the temperature in the product record today. Have Meridane reset the container now at sea and the one queued for 10 Oct. Add a check comparing booking temperature with the product specification. Do not suspend growers, file the cargo claim, revert the fungicide, or penalise the contractor yet. The cooperative's own sign-off reviewed the product record. Confidence is high.

Hold off on the claim, the suspension and the fungicide switch. Independent loggers are optional. I'm fairly confident in this diagnosis.

Dryer D5 has degraded, with dew point around −16 to −19 °C, and it can no longer dry that resin enough. Press 5 on Arnholt rejects about 10%. Arnholt on Press 7, which has a healthy dryer, rejects 0.8%. Quillan on Press 5 rejects 0.9%. Arnholt from lot A-2291 dried in a good portable dryer and fed to Press 5 rejected 0.8%, against 10.4% through D5. Second shift looks worse only because all its VX runs on Press 5. New and experienced operators have the same rates on each resin, so the operators are not the cause. Do not put them on improvement plans. Dropping Arnholt is also unnecessary. Do this week: repair D5 (heater and desiccant) and confirm −40 °C. Restore the original alarm limit. Keep Arnholt off D5 until it is verified. Add a moisture check at the press feed throat for every resin lot. Whether the unconditioned north annex storage adds moisture is untested, because Arnholt was only ever stored there. Don't pay for outside warehouse space until that is tested. I'm fairly confident in the main finding.

Millbrook kept its coordinator and staff booked 78–84 regulars a week. Its numbers are steady (118 to 111). Dock Street and Westgate lost their coordinators on 1 May and bookings fell from 74 a week to 3. Counts there roughly halved. At Dock Street and Westgate, 88% of regulars who lost their slot are now inactive, against 11% who kept it. 121 of 123 lapsed volunteers had a current background check, so renewal and Commonplate are minor. I'm fairly confident, though the evidence is observational. Do not cancel RotaWeave. It would cost $14k and not touch the cause. Do not suspend the checks or purge the rosters. Instead, use the idle admin seat to book regulars into their usual slots at Dock Street and Westgate. Phone the lapsed regulars to offer their old slots back. Review the results after 60 days. Consider asking the vendor about recurring bookings.

The Android drop is almost certainly caused by a new vendor rule, not by release 6.14. Corvane's 3 March rule-pack update added a rule (AUTO-LIB-17) that blocks password logins from the app's networking library when no edge session cookie is present. Blocking began at 10:41 UTC, a minute or so after the pack went live. The failures are HTTP 403s on password submissions only, on every app version, OS version and patch level. Version 6.14 is only 5% of attempts and fails at the same rate as older versions, so a rollback would not help. The blocked requests come from about 41,300 real installs, and 92% of them had logged in successfully before. iOS, web and quick-unlock are unaffected. That does not look like bot traffic. Next step: ask Corvane to put that rule into log-only mode on the mobile password path, keeping all other protections, then check that password-login success recovers. Don't raise bot sensitivity or drop blocked attempts from the KPI. Both would hide or worsen the problem. Continue the 6.14 rollout. I'm fairly confident (about 90%). Ask Corvane for the rule logic and a fix for the missing cookie condition.

Don't roll back gateway 5.8. The latency regression comes from the 2 Nov storage compaction tuning change, not the gateway. Per-cell data shows every cell that received the compaction push (FC-7710) jumped to about 300 ms within minutes. aps-3, which skipped the push but did get 5.8, stayed at 94 ms. A test rollback of euw-1 to 5.7 changed nothing (291 → 297 → 293 ms). Storage nodes after the push show compaction at 6 threads, disk at 97% utilisation, read queue wait of 205 ms, and node-side GET time up from 61 to 262 ms. Network and traffic growth don't fit the timing. A rollback would take about 4 hours and would reopen the signature vulnerability (SEC-2291) without fixing latency. Next step: revert the compaction change in one cell first (aps-3 is the control), watch p99 and backlog, then extend to the other cells. Don't pause compaction fleet-wide. Backlog is 11.2% and nearing the 15% danger point, so monitor it, and revisit Orrin rate limiting if backlog nears 15%. Backlog growth sources are not yet attributed (job reports 10 Nov). Confidence is high on the cause, moderate on backlog origin.

The same gap appeared in all five recent rollouts, including a config-only redeploy, and it adds only 10–20 errors. So it doesn't show that v4.18 is faulty. The dashboard counts agree with raw log recounts, so this isn't a counting artefact. I'm fairly confident (about 75%) the week is ordinary variation. Record the week as within the normal band and run the standard check on the following week. If the next week lands above the band, or the burn-rate page fires, open an incident then.

The complaints are most likely caused by water-contaminated brake fluid, not driver technique and not the new pads. All 11 Eastgate vans with complaints were serviced at Northfield Motor Services during the bay closure. Eleven of those 13 vans got fluid from an old bulk drum that had been opened in March and had a missing cap. The two Northfield vans that got fluid from a new drum have no complaints. Two vans were retested on 24 September and the fluid boiled at about 150°C, against 255°C for sealed stock. Drivers who complained also drove other vans on the same hilly routes without problems. That rules out technique and routes as the main cause. Pads on Calder Road vans and in-house vans show no matching problem. The garage warned Larkspur on 25 September and got no reply.

Next steps:
1. Pull every Northfield-serviced van from service now.
2. Test the fluid and renew it from sealed stock.
3. Check the two new-drum vans too, to be safe.
4. Do not discipline drivers. Their reports were accurate, and punishing them will stop people reporting.
5. Treat the pad squeal as a separate, lower-priority question.

I'm fairly confident, around 85–90%. The remaining unknown is how many vans are affected beyond those reported.

The wrong dates were not an operator or printer problem. Printer records show that from 4 Oct (22:10) every Veltranol job received a 36-month shelf life from PackBridge, before any operator touched it. Nobody overrode anything, including two permanent-staff jobs on Line 1. Jobs by agency operators after the firmware change, up to 3 Oct, were correct. The ERP shows Regulatory Affairs entered 36 months on 3 Oct, valid only from 1 Mar 2027, while the current value stays 24. The most likely cause is that the future-dated value reached the line early, despite the vendor's claim that this can't happen. I'm fairly sure, but the exact mechanism inside PackBridge is unconfirmed. The director's plan to remove and warn agency staff would punish the wrong people and leave the fault in place. Do now: lock the Veltranol shelf-life record to 24, hold all Veltranol lots packed since 4 Oct, including the two Line 1 lots in the warehouse, add a second-person expiry check at each setup, and check other products with future-dated edits (HX-15-30, MR-05-14). Ask the vendor to explain the behaviour. Keep the camera check, because it does verify print against the job. A wider 12-month reconciliation isn't justified now.

The wrong expiry dates are not an operator problem. Printer records show every Veltranol job from 2 Jun to 3 Oct had a 24-month shelf life and a correct expiry. The 4 jobs after the firmware change were correct, and so were the 3 run by agency operators. Two bad jobs ran on Line 1 day shift with permanent staff. On 3 Oct Regulatory Affairs entered a shelf life of 36 months for Veltranol, valid only from March 2027. The system should have ignored it until then, but the line data carried it from the next day. The vendor's claim that it cannot send future values is therefore contradicted by the records. Don't warn or remove the agency staff, and don't switch off the camera checks. Instead:
- Fix the ERP record.
- Extend the hold to all Veltranol lots since 4 Oct, including the two in the warehouse.
- Add a second-person check at setup.

The August drop is almost entirely explained by the cooling failure on floors 6-8. Chiller CH-2 was down from 4 to 19 August. Rooms there ran 26-29 C. Floors 6-8 room-comfort scores fell from 8.4 to 6.1. Their overall score fell to 6.8 for checkouts during the outage and recovered to 8.4 once cooling was restored. Of the 74 negative comments, 56 were about heat, all from those floors. Floors 1-5 were essentially flat. Cleanliness scores, inspection pass rates and kiosk metrics did not move, and the survey method was unchanged. So there is no evidence against Orrin or the kiosks, and I would not serve notice or pull the kiosks. The rate rise may have added a little to the value-for-money dip on floors 1-5, but that dip is close to the usual August seasonal pattern, so the rate rise is unproven. I would not reverse it yet. Next steps: reinstate the deferred preventive maintenance on both chillers, stock critical spares, and write a guest-recovery protocol for cooling outages. Keep the August scores as they are, because excluding the outage month would hide a real failure. Guests already received an apology and a credit, so a return-stay offer is optional. I'm confident in this diagnosis. I haven't collected extra evidence, and more is unlikely to change these steps.

Level 2 averages are unchanged since the lot change (5.81 before, 5.80 after). Re-running 43 patient samples on Analyzer A gave differences of about +0.02 mmol/L, all within allowable limits. All QC ran on schedule (182 of 182), so the short-staffing theory isn't supported. I can't say whether a sampling glitch caused it, because the instrument doesn't flag partial aspirations on that line.

Ward 6's high potassiums look unrelated to the analyzers. Half the high results came from Analyzer A. Transport delays were longer for the high results (11 of 14 over 3 hours). The tube outage and four renal overflow patients are confounders, and no repeat samples have been requested.

The evidence points to a single chance QC outlier on Analyzer B, not a faulty analyzer or bad reagent lot. Only Level 2 failed. Levels 1 and 3 and sodium and chloride passed. The repeat passed 21 minutes later. Level 2 mean is unchanged after the lot change (5.81 before, 5.80 after). Patient results on Analyzer A matched Analyzer B within 0.02 mmol/L on average, and the patient moving median is normal. QC ran on schedule (182 of 182), so the skipped-QC theory isn't supported. A transient sampling glitch is possible, because the analyzer can't flag partial aspirations, but it can't be confirmed. Don't record it as confirmed.

Ward 6's high potassiums are split evenly between Analyzers A and B. They coincide with the tube outage (delayed samples) and four renal overflow patients. Delay is the likelier explanation, but it isn't proven.

Recommended sign-off:

The rise in cancellations is mostly not a pricing problem. It comes from the Quillbook accounting connector. Quillbook retired its old invoice interface on 30 March, and since then the connector has silently dropped or doubled invoices. 1,212 of 1,900 Quillbook accounts were hit, and 34% of those have cancelled, against 8% of the unaffected ones. - Contact all Quillbook accounts, including those that cancelled, to correct their invoices.
- Make the connector's WARN-level failures visible on the health panel.
- Keep the duplicate-invoice hold. Switching it off would put duplicate invoices into customers' books.
- Don't roll back the price.
- Don't start the Tallymarsh rebuild yet. First review its log, since the signal there is tiny.

The gap is mostly a time-in-level effect, not a location effect. Only 32% of remote staff had the 18 months in level that the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. That is because remote hiring opened widely in July 2024, and 215 of the 340 remote staff started after March 2025. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28% vs 29%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and promotion rates (20% vs 21%) are nearly the same. The remote shortfall among eligible staff is about 1 point, and it rests on only 110 people, so a small real difference can't be ruled out. Remote staff don't leave more often than office staff (10.9% vs 11.6%). Remote staff are not concentrated in low-promotion job families. Don't adopt the three-day office rule. It would penalise people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misleading comparison. Do this instead: hold the proposal, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Some manager comments suggest remote staff get less visible work, but we have no data on that, so look at staffing records next. Confidence is fairly high on the main finding.

The crash gap is mostly not caused by the Tiled Canvas flag. Everyone on build 7.4.0 crashes at about 2%, including before the flag ramp began, while 7.3.2 stays near 0.7%. Within 7.4.0, flagged users (2.10%) and the random flag-off holdout (1.98%) are close. The difference is within noise, so a small flag effect, a few tenths of a point, can't be ruled out. Device mix and usage are the same across groups, and the app store's own crash counts match the crash-reporting tool's. The leading crash cluster is a native crash in the upgraded image library (Pixelda, HEIF decoding), at 41% of events. It first appeared on 2 Sep and doesn't occur in 7.3.2. Canvas code doesn't appear in any cluster. Flag users only look worse because only 7.4.0 users can get the flag. Don't turn the flag off and release 7.4.0 to 100% on the 18th. That would spread the real crashes to everyone. Hold the rollout at 25% and fix the image-library crashes. Keep the flag holdout running (or widen it) to settle the small flag effect, and don't close the incident. I'm fairly confident, though not certain which exact code path in the image library triggers the crashes.

The jump in chilled write-offs is mostly an internal problem, not a Haverlow problem. Since the night receiving team was cut from six to four in week 31, night pallets wait a median of about 3h50 between unloading and reaching a chiller (it was 44 minutes before). They sit in unrefrigerated dock lanes at 15–17°C. Night-shift write-offs rose from 0.6% to 2.9%, and the rate is the same for Haverlow, Pellridge and own-label. Day-shift write-offs are flat. Haverlow's trailer data, which can't be edited, shows product at 2.4–3.5°C when the doors open. The chambers also held temperature. The warm receipt probe readings were taken after the dock delay, so they don't show how the product left the trailer. Don't raise the chargeback or move volume. Dropping the night probe would hide the problem. Restore the night team to six, or otherwise fix the dock-to-chamber time. Set a maximum dock-to-chamber time and track it weekly from the scan data. Separately, ask Corriebank for its claim-level data to see how much of the credit rise is over-claiming. That part is unproven, and part of the rise may come from the same warming. I'm fairly confident about the main cause, and less sure about the credits.

The rise in delayed alarm responses comes mainly from the 12 August move of the alarm-forwarding server, not from agency staff. The hardware move was reported as like-for-like. In fact 11 of 14 forwarding rules were silently skipped, including the 15-second hold-off for brief SpO2 dips, repeat suppression, and routing technical alarms to the charge phone only. Phone notifications per nurse in Pods A–C roughly doubled from 12 August and acknowledgement times doubled. Pod D, still on the old server, saw no change. Incident rates there stayed flat even with a similar share of agency staff. Core nurses and agency nurses had similar rates after the change. Bedside alarm volume was flat, which argues against acuity and the monitor update. Core nurse sick leave rose later, probably partly from the respiratory virus season. A link to the alarm load is plausible but not proven. I am fairly confident (about 85–90%). Next step: restore the rules (about 4 hours plus validation), with Clinical Engineering and the Alarm Committee signing off. Then track notifications per nurse and acknowledgement times weekly. Don't cap agency use or open performance reviews, and don't stop phone forwarding of SpO2 alarms. Also check Pod D phase 2 isn't migrated before the rules are restored.

Add a check of reefer settings against the product specification before each submission. Hold the claim, the suspension and any invoice deduction. Loggers are a reasonable extra control.

The rejects come from an interaction, not from any single party. Arnholt resin arrives wetter (about 0.27–0.33% moisture, against a 0.20% molding limit) and the Press 5 dryer (D5) is degraded, so it can't dry it enough. Arnholt through D5 gives about 10% rejects. Arnholt through Press 7's healthy dryer gives 0.8%. Quillan through D5 gives 0.9%. The same Arnholt lot dried in a good portable dryer and run on Press 5 gave 0.8% rejects. The new operators are not the cause. Their reject rates match the experienced operators' on each resin. The higher second-shift rate only reflects that second-shift VX runs entirely on Press 5. Don't discipline the operators, and don't drop Arnholt outright.

Do this week: repair D5 (heater and desiccant), restore its original alarm limit, and verify the dew point is back to −40 °C. Until then keep Arnholt off D5. Add a moisture check at the press for every resin lot. Open question: Arnholt's wetter arrival may be due to storage in the unconditioned north annex or to the supplier, and the evidence can't separate the two. Test that before paying for warehouse space. Confidence is high on the main finding.

The Android login drop is almost certainly caused by a new vendor rule, not by release 6.14. On 3 March at 10:38 UTC, Corvane's automatic rule-pack update added a rule that blocks requests from the networking library our Android app uses on the password-login path. The first blocks were logged at 10:41. Every Android version dropped at that moment, including the 95% of users who don't have 6.14. The OS patch status made no difference. Quick-unlock is unaffected. About 41,300 installs were blocked, and 92% of them had logged in successfully before, so these are real customers and not bots. Rolling back 6.14, reverting the password screen, raising bot sensitivity, or excluding blocked attempts from the KPI would not fix this. The last two would make it worse or hide it. Next step: ask Corvane today to set the new rule to log-only on the mobile password path. Keep rate limits, lockout and the other rules on. Then check in telemetry that password success returns to about 96%. Ask Corvane to exempt the app's library signature permanently. Require testing of vendor rule changes. I'm fairly confident, and the data supports this.

Northfield warned Eastgate's workshop on 25 Sep and got no reply.

Confidence is high, but only two vans have actually been tested, so test them all.

The earlier price pattern by account size came about because bigger accounts are more likely to use Quillbook. The Tallymarsh numbers are small and look like normal variation, but nobody has reviewed that connector's log.

Next: make the Quillbook v3 fix the top engineering priority, and contact every Quillbook-connected account, including those who have left, to correct their invoices. Keep the duplicate-invoice hold on, because it stops duplicates reaching customers' books. Do not roll back the price or start the Tallymarsh rebuild yet. Instead, have someone review the Tallymarsh log. Make the sync warnings visible on the health panel. Confidence is high, though the price effect is not fully ruled out.

The remote promotion gap is mostly a matter of tenure, not location. Only 32% of remote staff have the 18 months in level that the policy requires, against 74% of office staff, because remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28% vs 29%) and approval rates (71% vs 74%) are almost the same, and remote 20.0% vs office 21.1% eligible-to-approved. Applying office rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, against 7.6% observed. Remote attrition is not higher, and the gap shows in every job family, so neither job mix nor exits explain it. I'm fairly sure the gap is mainly an eligibility effect. The eligible remote group is only 110 people, so a real proximity effect of a few points can't be ruled out. The manager comments about handing urgent work to nearby staff are anecdotal and untested. Don't adopt the three-day office rule. It would penalise people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Next: hold the proposal, report promotion rates for eligible people only, and check stretch-assignment allocation (staffing records) and the Committee's deferrals. Re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Briefings on the promotion criteria are reasonable but secondary.

The remote promotion gap is mostly a time-in-level effect, not a location effect. Policy requires 18 months in level to be nominated. Only 32% of remote staff meet that, against 74% of office staff, so the remote group is newer. Among eligible people, the rates are nearly the same: 20.0% remote and 21.1% office. Nomination rates (28% vs 29%) and committee approval rates (71% vs 74%) are also close. The gap appears in every job family because the tenure mix differs in every family, not because of proximity bias. Caveat: only 110 remote employees are eligible, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. I did not test whether remote staff get fewer high-visibility assignments, or whether they leave at a higher rate. Manager comments hint at the first, and the second is unmeasured. Recommendation: don't announce the three-day office rule. It would penalise people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Meanwhile, look at assignment allocation and attrition data. Confidence is moderately high.

The crash gap is mostly not caused by the Tiled Canvas flag. Build 7.4.0 crashes at about 2% from its first days (2 Sep), before the flag ramp, while 7.3.2 stays near 0.7%. Only 7.4.0 users can get the flag, so the flag and the build are tangled together. Inside 7.4.0, flagged users (2.10%) and the random flag-off holdout (1.98%) differ by only 0.12 points, and that difference is within noise. Device memory and usage are about the same across the groups. The top crash cluster is a Pixelda image library native crash (41% of events) that appears only in 7.4.0, and the app store's own crash counts confirm the gap. The sync-service deploy and the crash-reporting SDK are not the explanation. A small flag effect of a few tenths cannot be ruled out. Don't go ahead with the plan to turn the flag off, close the incident and release 7.4.0 to everyone: that would ship the real defect to everyone. Hold 7.4.0 at 25%, fix the Pixelda crash first, and keep the existing holdout, or widen it, to measure the flag's small effect. Confidence is fairly high on the build being the cause and moderate on the flag's own effect.

The evidence points mainly to Callerby's own decision, not Halden's behaviour. The tower crane was taken off site in October 2025 and sent to the Kestrel job. It stayed away until April. Frame work restarted on 6 April, soon after the crane came back. The site diaries say "on hold – design" every day, but never say what information was missing. The independent RFI platform shows the architect answered 62 of 64 queries on time. The draft claim's "late" count comes from the date Callerby opened a draft, not the date it submitted. The two genuinely late answers were on non-critical finishes. Halden's change orders may have caused some real delay, but that isn't quantified, and the 17-week figure is unproven. Don't send the claim as drafted: it rests on a misleading measure and risks credibility, and potentially a dishonesty finding. Don't discipline the superintendent. He told the truth, and a warning would look like suppression. Don't suspend the incentive scheme yet. Nothing shows it motivated the transfer. Next: get an independent delay analysis using the platform's submission timestamps and the change-order dates. Ask for more time before 1 December. Separately, review how plant is moved between projects. Also review how claims are checked before they go out.

The jump in chilled write-offs is mainly caused by the night receiving cut from six to four people in late July, not by Haverlow or the chambers. Night pallets now wait about 3 h 50 min from unload to chamber, up from 44 min. The dock staging area is unrefrigerated and averages 15–17°C overnight. Night write-off rates rose from 0.6% to 2.9% for every supplier, Haverlow, Pellridge and own-label alike. Day shift stayed flat. Haverlow's trailer logs show product at 2.4–3.5°C when the doors opened. The 6.5–8°C readings were keyed after the long dock wait, so they show warming at the DC, not at the supplier. The chambers held temperature. Don't raise the chargeback or move volume. It would penalise the wrong party and leave the cause in place. Don't drop the night probe either, because that would hide the problem. Restore six night operatives, or otherwise fix the dock-to-chamber delay, and set a maximum dock-to-chamber time for chilled pallets, tracked weekly from scan data. Separately, sample Corriebank's claims against lots and receiving shift. Self-certified credits may be inflated, but the evidence doesn't show it, and some of the rise may be real spoilage from the same delay. I'm fairly confident (about 85%) in the main finding.

The rise in delayed alarm responses is most likely caused by the 12 August move of the alert relay server, not by agency nurses. The import skipped 11 of 14 forwarding rules, including the 15-second hold-off for brief SpO2 dips, repeat-alarm suppression, and routing of technical alarms to the charge phone only. Pods A-C then went from about 38 to about 82 phone alerts per nurse per shift, and acknowledgement time doubled. Pod D, still on the old server, did not change. Incidents rose equally for core, agency and new-graduate nurses in the affected pods, and monitor alarm volume was flat, so acuity and the September monitor update don't explain it. The risk is alarm fatigue, which probably also contributes to the higher sick leave, though that link is unproven. I'd reject the agency cap and the performance reviews, because they would punish the wrong people. I'd also reject stopping phone forwarding of SpO2 alarms. Restore the old rules with Clinical Engineering validation and committee sign-off, then track alerts per nurse and acknowledgement times weekly. Confidence is high. Wireless coverage was not directly tested, but the pattern doesn't point to it.

The rejections trace to a data error in the new documentation suite, not to the fungicide, Meridane's equipment, the route, or Lower Serra growers. The mandarin product record was copied from an avocado record on 1 Aug, and its 7.0°C carriage temperature was never changed. The specification is 4.0°C. Every Tallis-booked Meridane container ran at 7°C and was rejected, with decay of 9–14%. Meridane's units held that setpoint, as its letter said. The earlier Meridane container (K1) was booked by email at 4°C, so it passed despite the 26-day transit. All Coastway containers at 4°C passed, including those packed with the new fungicide. K3 used old fungicide and still failed. Lower Serra fruit did decay more within rejected containers. That is not shown to be a cause, because accepted containers were not surveyed. I'm quite sure of the main finding. Next steps: correct the product record to 4.0°C now. Have Meridane reset the container at sea and the one queued for 10 Oct. Add a pre-submission check of reefer settings against the specification. Do not file the cargo claim, suspend Lower Serra, or revert the fungicide. Warn the importer.

The problem is concentrated in Kestrel, not in pay or the firm-wide hours target. Eight of the 11 associates on Kestrel resigned, against 1 of 13 who were not on it. Other groups' attrition is flat, so ordinary market movement and the January target change don't explain it. Pay doesn't explain it either: the group sits at the same salary percentile as the rest of the firm, the rival firm's band is £3–5k higher (not £15k), and most leavers took equal or lower pay. A retention payment would cost £228k and probably wouldn't fix it. I'd advise against announcing it or closing the review.

What I can't tell is whether the cause is the workload on Kestrel or how Dorian Faulk supervises. All 11 Kestrel associates reported to him, so the records can't separate the two. The survey comments point to both. I'm moderately sure of the Kestrel link and unsure which of the two is the cause. Next step: commission the roughly £9k confidential external interviews, set up to separate supervision from workload. Start adding matter and supervising-partner fields to attrition reporting. Then choose between moving supervision and adding contract reviewers. Document review runs to December 2026, so keep the interviews quick.

The rejects come from an interaction. Arnholt resin arrives wetter (0.27–0.33% against a 0.20% limit), and the Press 5 dryer (D5) is degraded, so it can't dry that resin enough. Neither factor alone causes the problem. Arnholt on Press 7 (good dryer) rejects 0.8%. Quillan on Press 5 rejects 0.9%. Arnholt through D5 rejects about 10%. The same Arnholt lot dried in a good portable dryer and run on Press 5 rejected 0.8%, against 10.4% through D5. The new operators are not the cause: second shift only looks worse because it runs only Press 5. Within Press 5, the new and experienced operators have the same rates on each resin. Don't put them on improvement plans. I'm fairly sure of this. The one gap is that Arnholt was stored only in the north annex, so supplier and storage are mixed together. That doesn't change what to do this week. Repair D5 (heater and desiccant), restore its −15 alarm limit to the original, keep Arnholt off D5 until D5 is verified at −40 °C, and check feed-throat moisture on every lot. Treat moving Arnholt out of the annex as a later question, and ask Arnholt about their moisture.

Cancelling RotaWeave probably won't fix this. The decline is concentrated at Dock Street and Westgate. Both sites got the app in April and lost their coordinator on 1 May. Millbrook has the app but kept its coordinator, and it is steady (118 to 111). Quarry Lane lost its coordinator but never went live on the app, and it is also steady (86 to 80). So neither change alone explains the fall. The combination does.

The mechanism is visible in the booking records. The basic app tier has no recurring bookings, so regulars only keep their usual slot if staff book them before the Thursday release. Staff did this for about 74 bookings a week until April. Since May it has been about 3 a week, and an admin seat sits unused. At Dock Street and Westgate, 88% of regulars who lost their slot at least twice are now inactive, against 11% of those who kept it. Callbacks mostly cite "nobody booked me".

Background-check renewal and Commonplate don't explain it. 121 of the 123 who lapsed held a current check, and only 2 of 61 callbacks mentioned joining another group.

Next steps: have staff or a trained lead volunteer book regulars into their usual slots at Dock Street and Westgate, and phone lapsed regulars to offer the slot back. Review after 60 days. Keep the renewal requirement. Don't purge the roster. Confidence is fairly high. The main gap is that the evidence is observational.

Confidence is fairly high, but the evidence is observational.

The Android login drop is not caused by release 6.14. It comes from a new vendor rule, AUTO-LIB-17, that arrived with Corvane's 3 March rule-pack update. The rule blocks password-login requests from the app's networking library when no edge session cookie is present. It started blocking at 10:41 UTC on 3 March and returns HTTP 403. About 41,300 Android installs were blocked, and 92% of them had logged in successfully in the prior 90 days, so these are mostly real customers. The failures are identical across every app version, including old ones, and across OS versions, with or without the March security patch. Quick-unlock is unaffected. Password success fell from 96% to 8%. The evidence for credential-stuffing, the OS patch, the new password screen and the auth-token change is weak or counts against each. I'm fairly sure of this, though I haven't seen Corvane's confirmation or a test with the rule switched off. Next step: ask Corvane to set the new rule to log-only on the mobile password path, keeping the other edge protections, rate limits and lockout in place, then check that password-login success recovers. Don't roll back 6.14, raise bot sensitivity, or exclude blocked attempts from the KPI.

FCR fell because of the 14 April Finance change, not the new starters. Agents' in-call credit limit dropped from £100 to £25, and larger adjustments now go automatically to the Billing Resolution team. Referrals on billing calls rose from 7% to 54% that same week. Referred calls resolve first time only about 34% of the time, against 82% for the rest. Billing FCR fell from 79% to 56%. Referral rates are about the same across tenure bands (53–56%). Tenured agents' FCR fell by the same amount (75% to about 67%). The April intake is only slightly lower, at 66.4%. Tariff enquiries are a bigger share of calls but still resolve at 85%. I can't rule out a small IVR effect, and I haven't established how much of the rise in complaints comes from the FCR fall. Don't put the April intake on performance plans: it would punish the wrong group. Run the credit-authority trial from Finance's own condition: a higher limit on two teams for six weeks, with post-call sampling, tracking FCR and unsupported credits. Don't restore the limit everywhere at once. Don't pause the IVR work on this evidence. MI can add referral breakdowns within a day, so the three-month dashboard rebuild isn't needed now. Confidence is fairly high.

The evidence points to the revised merit scholarship schedule, not the Admissions Office, as the main reason for the enrolment drop. Applications, admits and GPA all rose, so the applicant pool was not the problem. Yield fell sharply only in the tiers where awards were cut: Dean's went from $14,000 to $9,000 and Merit from $9,000 to $5,000. Yield was flat for Presidential awards, which were unchanged, and for students with no merit award. Early-action students got decisions on time yet their yield fell almost as much as regular-decision students' (7.4 vs 7.5 points). That argues against slow decisions as the main driver. The regular-decision delays were real, and the cause of them is unresolved. Reader cuts and the unstable portal module overlapped, and nobody has measured which mattered more. The missing-transcript complaints are unverified. I am fairly confident, though the data is not split by round within each tier. Next steps: do not replace the director on this evidence. Take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee with a modelled proposal to restore awards in the tiers where yield fell, before award letters go out. Also set a turnaround target for regular decisions, and audit the transcript problem before ordering any vendor rebuild.

Don't roll back the gateway. The latency jump comes from the storage compaction tuning change pushed fleet-wide on the evening of 2 Nov, not from gateway 5.8. In every cell that received the push, latency rose within minutes, even in cells still running gateway 5.7. One cell (aps-3) skipped the push but did get 5.8, and its latency stayed at about 94 ms. Rolling euw-1 back to 5.7 changed nothing. Storage-node data fits: compaction took 71% of disk bytes, disks hit 97% utilisation, and node-side GET time went from 61 to 262 ms. The network shows no fault. Traffic growth was small. A rollback would cost about 4 hours, leave the problem in place, and reopen the signature security hole. Next step: revert the tuning in one cell first and watch GET p99 and compaction backlog, then extend the revert if both behave. Backlog is about 11% against a 15% danger line, so watch it closely. Don't pause compaction entirely. Rate-limiting Orrin is an optional backstop; the source of backlog growth is still unattributed until the 10 Nov report. I'm fairly confident, about 85%.

Store 14's rise from 1.5% to 2.3% rests on interim estimates extrapolated from cycle counts. Those estimates carry roughly ±0.6 points of error per quarter. Across the chain, about half of stores that showed two consecutive rises of this size were not confirmed by the year-end full count. Store 14's past full counts were steady at 1.5–1.8%. The rise in recorded shoplifting incidents is also seen chain-wide, after a new incident app launched on 1 April, so it isn't good evidence of more theft at store 14. The ethics-line tip was checked against CCTV and was not substantiated. The sales mix hasn't changed, so that explanation is out. Self-checkout and the bus interchange are plausible but unproven. Neighbouring stores show no matching rise, but that doesn't settle which factor matters.

Next steps: keep store 14 in the 7 December full count. Don't pull the self-checkout lanes, hire a guard, or discipline anyone until that result is compared with the interim figures. Decline the proposal to skip the count, because it would remove the only reliable check. If the full count confirms a real rise, investigate causes then. I'm moderately confident in this.

Across the chain, about half of two-quarter interim rises of this size were not confirmed by the year-end full count. Store 14's own full counts have been stable at 1.5–1.8%. The rise is also spread across 61 of 74 product classes, and department sales mix was stable. That does not point to one cause. The shoplifting log counts are unreliable as a trend: the incident app launched chain-wide on 1 April, and recorded incidents rose chain-wide while chain shrink stayed flat. The ethics-line tip was checked against CCTV and showed cardboard bale runs, not theft. Self-checkout and footfall coincide in time with the rise, but that does not show cause. My recommendation is to keep store 14 in the 7 December full count and decline Regional Operations' proposal to skip it. Hold off on pulling the lanes, hiring a guard, or taking any action against the night stocker until the count result is compared with the interim figures. Extra cycle counts add little. Confidence is moderate to high on the action and lower on the individual causes.

The rise to 0.41% is most likely ordinary week-to-week variation. Over the previous 26 weeks the rate averaged 0.354% with a normal upper edge of 0.482%. Three earlier weeks went higher (0.44, 0.47, 0.51), and the investigations of those found nothing. The dashboard counts match raw log counts, so this is not a counting artefact. The burn-rate page did not fire (0.82x against a 2x threshold). Customers were not visibly affected: bookings were flat, no complaints came in, and retries recovered about 98.6% of failed requests.

The finding that new pods error at nearly twice the rate of old ones is a rollout warm-up effect. It appears in all five recent rollouts, including a config-only redeploy of unchanged code. New pods start with empty caches and time out against the database. That adds only 10–20 errors per rollout. It does not show that v4.18 is faulty.

I can't rule out the replica host move or partner-sync month-end load as small contributors. Neither is needed to explain the week.

Next steps:
- Don't roll back.
- Don't mute alerting. Muting the burn-rate page would remove a protective control.
- Note the week at ops review and apply the standard check to the following week.
- If next week exceeds the band, investigate then.
- Consider cache pre-warming for rollouts.

The Kestria buffering rise is almost certainly caused by the smart-TV app 5.2 release, not the CDN switch. Smart-TV 5.2 sessions stall 5.9% of the time. Every other client, including the 5.1 TV app, web, iOS and Android, stalls 0.6–0.7%. All of these run on the same new CDN, and the pattern is the same across all three ISPs. The stalls began on 9 October, when 5.2 went live, as the CDN cutover finished. The handball launch came later and nothing changed on its match nights. Moving traffic back to Corvane would not fix this, and an SLA notice with withheld fees would punish the wrong party. Do not mute the alert; it is the only warning we have. Next steps: revert the Kestria TV app's adaptive-streaming behaviour to the 5.1 settings and hold the wider 5.2 rollout until the regression is fixed. Add app version and device breakdowns to the dashboard, with an interim manual report until the rebuild. Do not give cancelled subscribers a free month yet. The exit survey has no streaming-quality option, and price is the top answer after the 1 October price rise, so buffering as a cause of cancellations is unproven. Confidence is high on the app being the cause and moderate on the cancellation link.

Don't send the breach notice. The rise in lost bags is not a handler problem. Pelion uses the same Tessaly crew pool and its rate didn't move. Corvane bags that were read automatically stayed at the old rate. The whole increase sits in bags diverted to the manual encode desk. Those diversions rose from about 70 to about 460 a day, and 91% of the affected bags reached the lateral after it closed. The cause is the tag stock. Brackwater tags used on counters on 14–16 Oct read normally, while kiosk tags printed on Fennick the same days still failed. Airport readers and other carriers' tags are unaffected. Hold off on any claim against Fennick until the test result is in. Optionally, ask the airport to add a temporary encode workstation for the evening bank. I'm fairly confident in this.

The complaints most likely come from contaminated brake fluid, not driver technique, the new pads or the hills. Northfield Motor Services changed fluid on 13 Eastgate vans during the bay closure. Eleven of them used a bulk drum that had taken on water, and those 11 vans are exactly the 11 vans with complaints. Two of them, retested on 24 Sep, had fluid boiling at about 150°C against 255°C for sealed stock. Wet fluid can vaporise on long descents and make the pedal go soft. The same drivers ran Upper Wend in other vans, 141 days, with no brake reports. Tessaro pads were also fitted at Calder Road and in-house, with no complaints from those vans. Northfield warned Larkspur on 25 Sep, and nobody replied.

Do this week: pull the Northfield-serviced vans from service, test and renew their fluid from sealed stock, then return them. LK-214 and LK-227 used a newer drum, so test them first. Drop the plan to discipline drivers, because it would suppress safety reports. Also tell the drivers who reported that they will not be disciplined. Hold off on changing pad supplier. Confidence is high. The main gaps are that I haven't seen Calder's fluid records and haven't tested fluid in the remaining Northfield vans.

Do now: fix the Veltranol shelf-life records so only 24 months can be read. Hold every Veltranol lot packed since 4 October, including the two warehouse lots. The August drop was mainly a cooling failure, not housekeeping or the kiosks. Chiller CH-2, which serves floors 6-8, failed on 4 August and wasn't fixed until 19 August. Rooms ran at 26.5-29 C. Analyzer B is very likely fine. One Level 2 potassium QC result failed. The re-pour passed 21 minutes later. Levels 1 and 3 were normal. Level 2 means are unchanged since the lot change. QC was run on schedule (182 of 182 runs). A single flag like this is expected by chance about once or twice a month. Patient samples re-run on Analyzer A agree within 0.02 mmol/L on average, and the patient median on B is stable. So the data don't support a lot problem, a systematic fault, or skipped QC. I can't say whether the cause was a sampling glitch or chance, and I wouldn't record either as confirmed.

Ward 6's high potassiums split evenly between the two analyzers. Most of them had samples delayed over 3 hours since the tube station failed. Four renal overflow patients also arrived. That points to transport delay and patient mix, not analyzer error. This link is likely but not proven. No repeat samples have been requested.

What to sign off: return B to service and close the 186-result review with no amendments. Keep the lot in use. Don't widen the limits and don't recall results. Consider an extra Level 2 QC at the start of each shift for a week. Ask Ward 6 for fresh samples from the high-result patients, and push for the tube repair.

The rise in cancellations is mostly not a pricing problem. It comes from the Quillbook accounting connector. Quillbook retired its old invoice interface on 30 March. Since then the connector has silently dropped or doubled invoices: 58,300 across 1,212 accounts. Of those accounts, 34% have cancelled, against 8% of Quillbook accounts with no recorded failure. Churn among Quillbook-connected accounts rose to about 6% a month, and the rise is the same for price-locked Founders accounts. Accounts with no connector are flat at about 1.9%, whatever their seat count, so the price rise shows no effect there. The finance seat-band pattern is explained by larger accounts being more likely to use Quillbook. Slow support responses are probably a contributing factor, but that is unproven. The Tallymarsh effect is within normal variation, though its error log hasn't been reviewed.

Next steps: make the Quillbook v3 fix the top engineering priority, and schedule it now (it is currently an unscheduled Sev-3 ticket). Contact every affected account, including those that cancelled, to correct their invoices. Keep the duplicate-invoice hold on. Don't roll back the price, which would cost about $220k a month. Don't start the Tallymarsh rebuild until its log has been reviewed. Confidence is high.

The gap is mostly a tenure effect, not where people work. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so most remote staff are new: only 32% of them had the 18 months in level the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28% vs 29%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and promotion rates (20% vs 21%) are nearly the same. Adjusting for eligibility gives an expected remote rate of 8.2% against the observed 7.6%. Remote staff do not leave more often. I can't confirm the proximity bias the COO described. The eligible remote group is only 110 people, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. Stretch-assignment access is untested; managers' comments hint at it. Don't adopt the three-day office rule. It would be built on a diagnosis the data don't support, and it would hit about 180 people hired on home-based contracts. Instead, hold the proposal and report promotion rates for eligible staff only. Re-check at FY2027, and collect staffing data on stretch work meanwhile. Confidence is fairly high on the main finding and moderate on the residual question of bias.

The flag could still add a few tenths of a point, so that remains unresolved. The flag is only available on 7.4.0, so the raw comparison of flagged users against everyone else was really 7.4.0 against 7.3.2. Device mix and usage are matched across groups, the sync-service deploy did not move the 7.3.2 rate, and the app-store console confirms the crash rates independently of the crash-reporting SDK. The leading crash cluster is a new Pixelda HEIF decode crash, first seen 2 Sep. It makes up 41% of crash events in 7.4.0 and does not occur in 7.3.2. Do not turn the flag off and release 7.4.0 to 100%, because that would ship the real crash source to everyone. Instead, hold the rollout at 25% and fix the Pixelda crash, and add the screen that requested the decode to the crash reports. Keep the existing holdout running to measure any flag effect. Don't roll back the crash-reporting SDK. Confidence is fairly high.

The Android login drop is almost certainly caused by a vendor rule update, not by release 6.14. On 3 March at 10:38 UTC Corvane activated a new edge rule, AUTO-LIB-17. It blocks (HTTP 403) password requests that use the nettle-http library and have no edge session cookie. The Android app uses that library for every API call. The first blocks appeared at 10:41. Telemetry shows password success fell from 96% to 8% on every app version and OS version at the same minute. Quick-unlock, iOS and web were unaffected. 6.14 was only at 5% of attempts, and its success matched older versions. Blocked requests came from about 41,300 installed-app IDs, 92% of which had logged in successfully in the previous 90 days, so these are real customers, not bots. Next steps: ask Corvane to set the new rules to log-only on the mobile password path, keeping the other protections on, and confirm recovery in telemetry. Don't roll back 6.14, raise bot sensitivity, or exclude blocked attempts from the KPI. Excluding them would hide the customer impact. Confidence is high. Contact-centre call volume was probably affected by the fee notices too, so that link is uncertain.

Early-action students got decisions and awards on the old timetable, and their yield fell by about as much (45.2% to 37.8%) as regular decision's (39.0% to 31.5%). Next steps: take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee with a costed proposal to restore awards in the tiers where yield fell, before award letters go out. The complaints most likely come from contaminated brake fluid, not driver technique, the new pads, or the hills. Northfield Motor Services changed fluid on 13 Eastgate vans while the in-house bay was closed. Eleven of those vans used an old bulk drum with a replaced cap. The two vans serviced from a fresh drum (LK-214 and LK-227) have no complaints. All 11 complaining vans are among the 13 Northfield vans, and no other Eastgate van has complaints. The same drivers had no problems in other vans, including on Upper Wend. Northfield recommended rechecking the other vans on 25 September, and nobody replied. I'm fairly confident (roughly 85–90%).

Next steps:
- Pull all 13 Northfield vans, test the fluid, and renew it from sealed stock. Include the two fresh-drum vans, since the cost is small.

QC ran on schedule, so the short-staffing theory isn't supported. Ward 6's high potassiums are split 7 and 7 between the two analyzers. They coincide with the tube outage, which caused long transport delays, and with four renal overflow patients. Both are likely explanations, though I haven't proven it.

What to sign off: return Analyzer B potassium to service and close the review of the 186 flagged results with no amendments. Optionally add extra Level 2 QC at the start of each shift for a week. Don't recall about 2,900 results, quarantine the lot, or widen the limits to ±4 SD, because that would hide real errors. Don't record "sampling disturbance" as confirmed, since it can't be proven. Tell Ward 6 to fix the tube delays and repeat-sample their high results. Confidence is moderate to good; I collected no further evidence.

What is going on: the VA-220 failures are mainly caused by defective 2026-built Pellacott valves, not by the new installers or firmware 4.2. Installer and firmware groups fail at the same rate (about 41 vs 42 and 40 vs 42 per 1,000), and Durrant-Hale valves are clean. The defect is a leaking slide seat in Pellacott's 2026 valves. Pellacott's certificates do not reflect real testing. Its leak rig LT-04 has been out of service since 9 January 2026, the 2026 certificates repeat a few identical value sequences, and the "backup rig" was never shown. That is why its score rose. How sure: fairly sure about the installer, firmware and certificate findings. Less sure whether the Corlin seal change is the cause, since it is confounded with the move to Line 3, and I did not check other suppliers. What to do now: quarantine all 2026 Pellacott VA-220 stock, including the six held lots. Suspend its dock-to-stock status. Test valves with Brenmoor's own helium leak test. Do not release the held lots on Pellacott's certificates. Do not charge back installers. Examine the other suppliers' test records before relying on them. Then test the seal material.

The proximity-bias story is not supported. Most of the gap comes from eligibility: remote staff are far less likely to have the 18 months in level needed to be nominated (32% of remote staff are eligible versus 74% of office staff). Among eligible employees, remote and office rates are close (20.0% vs 21.1%), and nominees are approved at similar rates (71% vs 74%). A small remaining gap could be chance, since the remote group is only 110 people. Do not announce the three-day office rule. It would penalise remote staff for a cause the data does not show, and it would affect about 180 people who live far away. Next, hold the proposal, and rebuild the reporting to compare eligible remote and office staff. Also look at why remote staff have less time in level, which may reflect recent hiring, and check who gets stretch work, since the current records cannot show it. My confidence in the eligibility finding is moderate-to-good. My confidence about stretch work and attrition is low because we have no data on them.

The remote promotion gap is mostly explained by eligibility, not by where people work. Remote staff are much less likely to have the 18 months in level needed to be nominated (32% eligible vs 74% office). Among eligible employees, the rates are nearly the same: 21.1% office versus 20.0% remote. Nomination rates (28.6% vs 28.2%) and committee approval of nominees (74% vs 71%) are also close. Job-family mix does not explain it either, since the mix is similar across arrangements. So the data does not support proximity bias as the main driver. Confidence is moderate. The remote comparison rests on 110 eligible people, and a small real gap cannot be ruled out. I did not check stretch-assignment access or attrition, so those remain open. Next steps: do not announce the three-day office rule, since it would penalise remote staff for a tenure artifact. Change promotion reporting to compare eligible staff only. Check whether remote staff are being given stretch work, and look at why remote staff have shorter time in level, such as recent hiring.

Change reporting to compare eligible people only, and re-check at FY2027. Meanwhile, look at stretch-work allocation and attrition. Confidence is moderate to high.

Next steps: do not submit the claim as drafted. Commission an independent forensic delay analysis now, before 1 December, and ask for a short extension from Halden if needed. Bedside alarm volume did not change, and agency share was similar in Pod D, which did not see a rise. Next steps: restore the original forwarding rules with Clinical Engineering validation, and track notifications and acknowledgement times weekly. Do not cap agency use or discipline nurses, and do not switch off phone forwarding of SpO2 alarms.

This week: repair D5's heater and desiccant, restore its original alarm limit, and verify the dew point before any Arnholt goes through it. Most of the drop is not caused by RotaWeave itself, nor by the background checks, nor by Commonplate. At Dock Street and Westgate, regulars who lost their weekly slot after the coordinator posts ended were usually not rebooked, and 88% of them are now inactive. Millbrook kept its coordinator and stayed flat on the app. Quarry Lane lost its coordinator but never went live on the app, and declined only modestly. The app and the coordinator loss together, with nobody booking regulars into their slots, appear to be the mechanism. Low June satisfaction is more likely a symptom than the cause. My confidence is moderate, since the link is mostly from booking records and callbacks, and Commonplate was not examined. Next steps: keep RotaWeave for now and do not cancel it before 30 September. Within the next two weeks, assign a named person at Dock Street and Westgate to rebook regulars into their usual slots before each Thursday release, and phone lapsed regulars to offer their old slots back. Do not suspend the background-check rule, which the county and insurer require. Do not remove inactive volunteers from the figures. Track re-engagement over 60 days.

Next: restore weekly-slot booking at Dock Street and Westgate now (reversible, low cost), and phone lapsed regulars. Do not suspend the background-check rule, which the county and insurer require. Do not cancel RotaWeave on 30 September, since the evidence does not show it is the cause and cancelling would cost $14,000 and lose attendance data. Remove nobody from the figures. What to do: have a staff member or trained lead volunteer book regulars into their usual slots at Dock Street and Westgate, and phone lapsed regulars to offer their slot back. Do not cancel the contract, suspend the checks, or purge the roster. My confidence is fairly high. The data is observational, but the pattern across sites is consistent.

The Android password-login drop is not caused by release 6.14 or by an Android OS update. It starts at 10:41 UTC on 3 March, about three minutes after the edge-protection vendor's rule pack 2026.03.1 went live. A new vendor rule, AUTO-LIB-17, blocks password requests on the Android app that carry the nettle-http client library signature. It returns HTTP 403, and it blocks about 6,000 to 9,800 requests a day from roughly 41,300 installs, 92% of which logged in successfully in the prior 90 days. These are mostly real customers, not bots. Quick-unlock and iOS are unaffected. Confidence is high for the edge rule as the main cause; the exact reason 6.12 and 6.13 are also hit is not yet explained. Credential stuffing (Security's theory) and the 14:00 session-timeout change are contradicted by the timing and the 403 pattern. The contact-centre rise is probably linked, but the fee mailing confounds it, so treat it as association only. Next steps: ask Corvane to set AUTO-LIB-17 to log-only on the mobile password path, keeping rate limits and lockout, and confirm recovery in telemetry. Do not raise bot sensitivity, do not exclude blocked attempts from the KPI, and do not revert the password screen.

Don't exclude blocked attempts from the KPI, raise bot sensitivity, or continue the rollout unchanged. Plan a durable fix with Mobile and Corvane. Pausing the IVR work is not justified by this evidence.

Do not replace the director on this evidence. Hold off on vendor remediation until the missing-document reports are verified.

Since the night receiving team was cut from six to four in week 31, chilled pallets wait about 3 hours 52 minutes (up from 44 minutes) on an unrefrigerated dock averaging 15–17°C. Night write-off rates rose from 0.6% to 2.9% for every supplier; day shifts stayed flat. Haverlow's trailer telematics, which can't be edited, show product at 2.4–3.5°C when the doors open. The "warm" receiving probe readings were keyed hours after unloading, so they measure dock warming. The chambers held temperature. I'm fairly confident (about 85%). Do not raise the chargeback or shift volume: it would penalise the wrong party and leave the cause in place. Do not drop night probing. Restore night staffing, or otherwise cap dock-to-chamber time, and monitor it weekly from scan data. Separately, reconcile a sample of Corriebank claims, since their self-certified credits rose from 3 August. Whether over-claiming is happening is still unknown, so don't ask for photo evidence yet. Fix the receiving process first.

The rise in delayed alarm responses most likely comes from the 12 August alarm-relay server move, not from agency nurses. The move was meant to be like-for-like, but 11 of 14 forwarding rules were silently skipped during import. These rules included the 15-second hold-off for brief low-SpO2 alarms, repeat-notification suppression, and routing of technical alarms to the charge phone only. Phone notifications per nurse roughly doubled in Pods A–C, and acknowledgement time doubled. Pod D, still on the old server, saw no change. Incidents rose equally for core, agency and agency-share-matched staff, and the agency share was similar in Pod D. Bedside alarm volume was flat, which rules out acuity and the monitor update (v7.2). Sick leave rising alongside the alarm load is plausible but unproven; a hospital-wide virus is a rival explanation. Recommendation: do not cap agency staff or open performance reviews. Do not switch off phone forwarding of SpO2 alarms. Restore the rules, with clinical validation and committee sign-off, then track notifications per nurse and acknowledgement times weekly. Confidence is high. Wireless coverage was not directly tested, but it does not explain the pod pattern.

The rejections were most likely caused by our own paperwork, not by the fungicide, the Lower Serra growers or Meridane. When Meridane bookings moved to the new Tallis system, the mandarin product record was copied from the avocado record, so every Meridane container was sent with a 7.0°C setting instead of our 4.0°C specification. The carrier's units held that setting within 0.4°C. All five Meridane containers with 7.0°C were rejected, with 9–14% decay. All four containers at 4.0°C passed, including Pellacor-treated ones and a Meridane one with the old fungicide. K3 was rejected with old-stock fungicide, and the 4.0°C Coastway containers carried Pellacor fruit and passed. That rules out the fungicide. Lower Serra fruit was worse within rejected containers, but it was never compared in accepted ones, so that link is unproven.
Next steps: fix the temperature in the mandarin product record now. Have Meridane reset the container at sea and the one queued for 10 Oct. Add a check of reefer settings against the product specification before each submission. Do not suspend Lower Serra, do not file the claim against Meridane, and do not go back to the old fungicide. Hold off on penalising the contractor until responsibility is reviewed, since our own sign-off also missed the error. Independent loggers are useful but secondary.

The rejects come from the combination of Arnholt resin and Press 5's degraded dryer (D5). Neither alone causes them. On Press 5, Arnholt runs about 10% rejects on both shifts. Press 5 on Quillan runs 0.9%. Press 7 on Arnholt runs 0.8%. The new operators match the experienced ones on each resin, so they are not the cause. Please don't discipline them. Arnholt arrives wetter at the dryer (0.27–0.33% against 0.11–0.14%). D5 can't dry it to the 0.20% limit. A healthy dryer (D7) can. The same Arnholt lot gave 10.4% rejects through D5 and 0.8% through a portable dryer at −40 °C. Do not drop Arnholt. Next steps: repair D5 (heater and desiccant), confirm −40 °C, and restore the original alarm limit. Until then, keep Arnholt off D5 and add a moisture check at the press throat for every resin lot. Arnholt was sampled only from the north annex, so I can't say how much storage adds to its moisture. Treat the annex as a separate question. Moving the octabins to rented space is premature. Running Arnholt only on Press 7 and leaving D5 broken would be an incomplete fix.

Volunteers did not leave because of the app alone, the background checks, or a rival group. They left where two changes overlapped. Dock Street and Westgate have the app and lost their coordinators on 1 May. The app's basic tier doesn't keep recurring weekly slots, so someone has to book regulars in before each Thursday release. Coordinators used to do that. Manual bookings fell from 74 a week to 3, and an admin seat sits unused. Of the 213 April regulars at those two sites, 129 lost their usual slot at least twice in May–June, and 114 of those have since gone inactive. Only 9 of the 84 who kept their slot are inactive. Millbrook has the app but kept its coordinator, and Quarry Lane lost its coordinator but has no app live and uses a paper roster. Both held steady. Background checks hit all sites equally, and 121 of the 123 who lapsed had current checks. Rival recruitment looks minor, with 2 of the 61 callbacks joining another group. Don't cancel RotaWeave, suspend the checks, or purge the roster. Assign someone to book regulars into their usual slots before each Thursday release at Dock Street and Westgate, and phone lapsed regulars to offer slots back. Review after 60 days. Confidence is fairly high. Be careful at Quarry Lane when the app goes live on 6 Oct.
