The Android login drop is almost certainly not caused by release 6.14. At 10:38 UTC on 3 March, Corvane auto-updated its edge rules. A new rule, AUTO-LIB-17, blocks any password-login request that uses the nettle-http library with no edge session cookie. That describes every Android app version, because the app uses nettle-http for all API calls. The rule returns a 403. It has blocked about 9,700 requests a day, from roughly 41,300 app installs, 92% of which had logged in successfully before. The failures began within a minute of the rule going live, on every app version and every OS version, whether or not the March security patch was installed. iOS, web and quick-unlock never match the rule. So the rollback of 6.14, the OS patch, the screen redesign, the auth token change and credential stuffing don't explain the drop. I'm quite confident (about 90%). Next: ask Corvane to switch AUTO-LIB-17 to log-only on the mobile password path, keeping rate limits, lockouts and other rules on. Then confirm in telemetry that password success recovers. Don't roll back 6.14. Don't raise bot sensitivity. Don't exclude blocked attempts from the KPI, because those are real customers.

FCR fell because of the 14 April Finance change, not the new starters. It cut agents' in-call credit limit from £100 to £25. Billing calls referred to the Billing Resolution team went from 7% to 54% that week. Referred calls resolve first time only about a third of the time (33–34%), against 82% for non-referred calls. Customers then call back for status. Referral rates are the same across tenure bands (April intake 56%, others 53–54%). Experienced staff fell from about 75% to about 67%, the same as the site. The new intake is therefore not the driver. Tariff calls rose in share but still resolve at 85%. The IVR change came two weeks after the drop, so it is not the cause. Don't roll it out everywhere at once. Don't pause the IVR work on this evidence. Ask MI to rerun the breakdown for the trial teams.

The enrolment drop is mostly a yield problem, and it is concentrated where the scholarship cuts were made. Applications and admits rose, so the applicant pool is not the cause. Yield held steady for Presidential awards (unchanged) and for students with no merit award. It fell about 13 points in the Dean's tier (award cut from $14,000 to $9,000) and about 12 points in the Merit tier (award cut from $9,000 to $5,000). Also set a turnaround target for regular-decision files and restore the merit-review reader posts. Hold off on a vendor rebuild until the missing-document claim is checked.

Don't roll back the gateway. The regression comes from the 2 Nov storage compaction tuning change, not from gateway 5.8. That push raised compaction threads from 2 to 6 and compaction's share of disk bytes from 38% to 71%. Disk utilisation went from 41% to 97% within five minutes in each cell. Node-side read time rose from 61 ms to 262 ms. Latency rose in each cell within minutes of its push, even in cells that still had 5.7 or only a few gateways on 5.8. The one cell that skipped the push (aps-3) already had 5.8 and stayed at about 94 ms. A test rollback to 5.7 in euw-1 changed nothing. Rolling back would also reopen the security hole and would not help latency. Network and traffic growth don't fit the timing.

Next: revert the compaction tuning in one cell first, watch p99 and compaction backlog, then extend it to the other cells. Don't pause compaction. Backlog was 11% against a 15% danger point, and a pause risks disk-full. Hold the Orrin rate limit until the 10 Nov attribution report shows where backlog growth comes from. The lifecycle sweep is a competing source. I'm fairly confident in the cause. The Orrin link is the least certain part.

The rise from 0.31% to 0.41% looks like ordinary week-to-week variation, not a fault in v4.18. Over the prior 26 weeks the rate averaged 0.354% with a normal-band upper edge of 0.482%. Weeks hit 0.51%, 0.47% and 0.45% with no fault found, and 0.41% is inside the band. The dashboard count matches raw logs, so it is not a counting artefact. The burn-rate page did not fire (0.82x against a 2x threshold). Booking completion was flat and there were no complaints. The rollout comparison that points at v4.18 is misleading. New pods start with cold caches and time out against the replica in every rollout. That includes an unchanged config-only redeploy and the four earlier releases, at 0.47–0.58% against 0.29–0.33% on old pods. It adds only 10–20 errors. So I would not roll back, and I would not mute the alerts. Muting would remove the protection that would catch a real problem. Record the week as within the normal band and apply the standard check to next week. If next week is above the band or the page fires, open an incident. The replica host change and partner-sync month-end traffic are not ruled out, but nothing here needs action. Confidence is fairly high but not complete.

The Kestria buffering is almost certainly caused by the smart-TV app 5.2 release, not the new CDN. The release lowered the player's startup buffer from 10 s to 4 s and let it switch up in quality after 2 s buffered. It went live in Kestria first, on 9 Oct, the same day as the CDN cutover. Rebuffering on 5.2 TVs is about 5.9% on every ISP. Every other client on the same CDN and ISPs sits at 0.6–0.7%. Employee test TVs in another market, served by the old CDN, showed 5.7% on 5.2 versus 0.6% on 5.1 before launch. The fix for that test was deferred. Handball viewing and ISP congestion don't fit the pattern. Recommendation: don't send the breach notice, withhold fees or move traffic back. That would punish the wrong party and leave the problem in place. Instead, revert Kestria to the old streaming settings (abr_v2 is a server-side remote-config profile, roughly an hour to take effect). Hold the 20 Nov wider rollout, and keep the rebuffering alert on. Then add app version and device breakdowns to monitoring. Hold the free-month offer until you've confirmed how much of the cancellation rise comes from buffering, since the 1 Oct price rise is also a likely factor. I'm confident in the main finding. The cancellation link is unproven.

Don't discipline drivers or retrain everyone. The evidence points to contaminated brake fluid. Northfield Motor Services changed the fluid in 13 Eastgate vans during the bay closure, mostly from an old bulk drum with a missing cap, and the drum had absorbed water. Two vans retested there on 24 Sep had fluid boiling at about 150°C, against 255°C for sealed stock. The 11 vans with complaints are all among the 13 Northfield vans. The two Northfield vans that got fluid from a fresh drum had no complaints. Pad batches were split about evenly between garages, and every van ran Upper Wend about as often. The same drivers reported no problems in other vans, so technique and hill routes don't explain it. Northfield's 25 Sep recommendation to recheck the other vans got no reply. I'm fairly confident, around 85–90%. Next: pull every Northfield-serviced van from service this week, boiling-point test it, renew the fluid from sealed stock, and then return it to the pool. Keep LK-209 parked until that is done. Tell drivers that reporting is safe. Consider checking the Calder Road vans and pad noise separately.

The evidence points to bad data, not operators or printers. On 3 Oct Regulatory Affairs entered a 36-month shelf life for Veltranol, valid only from 1 March 2027. The old 24-month value is still the one in effect. Yet from 4 Oct the line integration service sent 36 months to the printers. Every job since then has an expiry 12 months too late. All 47 Veltranol jobs show no operator overrides. The printer printed exactly what it received. The camera passed every carton because it only checks print against the job. Jobs before 4 Oct were correct, including those after the firmware change and those set up by agency operators. Two jobs on Line 1 day shift, run by permanent staff, were also wrong. Why the future-dated value was used is not yet established. That is the vendor's claim versus the evidence.

Do not discipline or remove the agency operators. Do not switch off camera checks. Reset the Veltranol record, extend the hold to every Veltranol lot packed since 4 Oct, including the two in the warehouse, and add a second-person check at setup. Check other products with October edits, especially the two with later valid-from dates. Ask the vendor to explain the behaviour. I'm fairly sure of the Veltranol cause. Other products are unchecked.

Inspect other products whose records changed in October, especially the two with future valid-from dates. Ask Corvane and IT to explain how PackBridge read the future value. Confidence is high on cause and moderate on how far it spreads.

The August drop is almost entirely explained by the east-riser chiller (CH-2) failure from 4 to 19 August. It left floors 6-8 at 26-29 C for about two weeks. Floors 6-8 room comfort fell from 8.4 to 6.1, and their overall score fell from 8.6 to 7.4. Scores recovered to 8.4 once cooling was restored. Floors 1-5 were flat. 56 of the 74 negative comments were about heat, all from floors 6-8. Cleanliness scores, inspection pass rates and kiosk metrics did not move, so neither Orrin nor the kiosks is implicated. Don't serve notice on Orrin and don't pull the kiosks. The survey questionnaire was unchanged. The 6% rate rise may have nudged value-for-money scores down on floors 1-5, but that is not separable from the usual August dip, so leave rates alone and keep watching. Next steps: reinstate the deferred maintenance on both chillers, stock critical spares, and write a guest-recovery protocol for cooling outages. A return-stay offer for affected guests is reasonable. They already received an apology and a half-night credit. Report August as it is; don't exclude the floors 6-8 responses. I'm fairly confident, and I collected no further evidence because more would be unlikely to change these actions.

Analyzer B most likely had a single chance QC outlier. The repeat from the same vial passed. Sodium, chloride and the other two potassium levels were fine. Level 2 means are unchanged since the lot change (5.81 before, 5.80 after). Only one flag appeared in a month, which fits the expected false-rejection rate. B and A agree on 43 patient samples (mean difference +0.02). B's patient median is steady. All 182 scheduled QC runs were completed on time, so the claim that short staffing led to skipped QC is not supported. A short sample or bubble can't be excluded, so don't record it as the confirmed cause.

Ward 6's high potassiums are split evenly between Analyzers A and B. They coincide with the tube outage, which caused long transport delays, and with four renal overflow patients. Delay is the likelier explanation, though that link is only an association so far. No repeat samples were requested.

What to sign off: return B to service and close the 186 results with no amendments. Optionally add extra Level 2 QC for a week. Don't recall results, quarantine the lot or widen the limits. Ask Ward 6 to send repeat samples and fix the tube station. I'm moderately confident in this.

Analyzer B most likely had one isolated potassium QC outlier: a chance flag or a one-off sampling glitch. The evidence points that way for five reasons. The other two QC levels passed. The repeat from the same vial passed. QC means are unchanged since the lot change. All 43 patient samples re-run on Analyzer A agreed within limits. B's patient median is normal. QC ran on schedule, so skipped QC is not supported. The Ward 6 highs are split 7 on A and 7 on B. Most of them had samples more than 3 hours in transit during the tube outage, and four renal overflow patients arrived at the same time. So the analyzers are probably not giving false highs. I'm less sure of the tube-delay explanation, because the renal patients could also account for it.

Recommended sign-off:
- Return B to potassium service and close the review of the 186 results with no amendments.
- Do not recall everything, because that means recollecting about 2,900 patients.
- Do not quarantine the lot.
- Do not widen the limits.
- Don't record a sampling glitch as the confirmed cause. It is only plausible.
- Optionally add extra Level 2 QC per shift for a week.
- Ask Ward 6 to repeat samples on the high results, and fix the tube station.

Confidence is moderate to high. I did not collect any further evidence.

The VA-220 failures trace to Pellacott's 2026-built valves, not to the new installers or firmware 4.2. The quality-lab data matched to serial numbers shows the same claim rate (about 41–42 per 1,000) for legacy and new installers and for firmware 4.1 and 4.2. Durrant-Hale valves stay at 5–7 per 1,000 in every group. Never-installed Pellacott 2026 valves leak at the seat 11% of the time, against 1% for 2025 builds and 0% for Durrant-Hale. The calibration contractor found Pellacott's leak-test rig out of service since January 2026, with no VA-220 test program on any other rig. Certificate values repeat four fixed sequences, which also appear in November 2025 certificates. So the certificates very likely do not reflect real tests. That also explains the score rise, since the score rewarded complete certificates. Do not release the six held lots on fresh certificates, and do not penalise the installers. Quarantine 2026-built Pellacott stock, suspend dock-to-stock, and run your own helium leak testing before release. Plan for line impact by sourcing more from Durrant-Hale. Check whether other suppliers' records are genuine, and tie scoring to rig logs. The seal change is a plausible mechanism but isn't separable from the line move. Confidence is high.

The cancellation rise is not mainly a pricing problem. It is concentrated in accounts connected to Quillbook. Their monthly churn went from about 2% to about 6%, and it is the same for price-locked Founders accounts and repriced accounts. Accounts with no connector, which are most of the base, are flat at about 1.9% whatever the seat count. The seat-size pattern in the finance analysis arises because Quillbook accounts are larger. Quillbook retired its old invoice interface on 30 March. Since then the connector has silently dropped or duplicated 58,300 invoices across 1,212 accounts. 34% of those accounts have cancelled, against 8% of accounts with no recorded failure. The health panel counts only ERROR, so these WARN events were never seen. Support is also slow, but that looks like a side effect.

Recommendation: don't roll back the price, which would cost about $220k a month and wouldn't fix this. Don't switch off the duplicate-invoice hold, because it has kept 3,870 duplicates out of customers' books. Make the Quillbook v3 migration (3–4 weeks) the top engineering priority. Contact every Quillbook account, including those that cancelled, to correct their invoices. Make the health panel count WARN events. Review the Tallymarsh log before committing a rebuild; its churn change is within normal variation. Confidence is fairly high, though this is observational data.

I'm fairly confident (about 85%). I'd recommend these steps:
1. Make the move to the v3 interface the top engineering priority.
2. Contact every Quillbook account, including those that already cancelled, to correct their invoices.
3. Keep the duplicate-invoice hold, because it has stopped 3,870 duplicates reaching customers' books.
4. Do not roll back the price.
5. Review the Tallymarsh log before committing a rebuild. Its churn change is within normal variation.

The promotion gap is mostly a tenure effect, not proof of proximity bias. Remote work was opened to all roles only in July 2024, so 230 of 340 remote staff (68%) have under 18 months in level and are ineligible under policy, against 26% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28.2% vs 28.6%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and promotion rates (20.0% vs 21.1%) are nearly the same. Applying office rates to the remote tenure mix predicts 8.2% remote, against 7.6% observed. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% vs 11.6%), and the gap shows in every job family, so job mix doesn't explain it. Caveat: only 110 remote staff are eligible, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. The interview and survey hints about uneven stretch work and less clarity on promotion criteria remain unverified. Recommendation: don't adopt the three-day office rule. It would exclude about 180 people hired on home-based contracts, and the evidence doesn't support it. Hold it, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at FY2027. Separately, check how stretch assignments are distributed, and consider briefing staff on promotion criteria. Confidence is fairly high on the main finding.

The remote promotion gap is mostly a tenure effect, not proof of proximity bias. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so most remote staff are new. Only 32% of remote employees had the 18 months in level that policy requires to be nominated, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, rates are nearly the same: 20.0% remote and 21.1% office. Nomination rates (28%) and approval rates (71% vs 74%) are also close. Remote attrition is no higher than office attrition, and the job-family mix does not explain the gap. The dashboard's raw rate divides by everyone, so it compares unlike groups.

Caveat: only 110 remote employees are eligible, so a real gap of a few points could still exist. The manager interviews hint that urgent work goes to nearby staff, and I found no direct data on stretch assignments. Proximity bias is therefore not ruled out, only unproven.

Do not announce the three-day office rule. It would bar about 180 remote staff hired on home-based contracts, and the evidence doesn't support it. Instead, change the reporting to compare eligible employees only, and re-check at FY2027. Look at assignment staffing data separately.

The crash gap is mostly not caused by the Tiled Canvas flag. Everyone who can get the flag is on build 7.4.0, and 7.4.0 crashed at about 2% from 2 September, before the flag ramp began. The 7.3.2 build stayed near 0.7% throughout. Within 7.4.0, flag-on users (2.10%) versus the random flag-off holdout (1.98%) differ by only 0.12 points, and the uncertainty range includes zero. Device mix and usage are the same across the groups. The largest crash cluster (41%) is a native crash in the upgraded Pixelda image library, which does not occur in 7.3.2. The app store's separate crash count agrees with the crash monitor, so this is not a counting artifact. The 9 September sync-service deployment did not change 7.3.2 rates.

Turning the flag off and shipping 7.4.0 to 100% would leave the real cause in place and spread it to everyone. Instead: hold 7.4.0 at 25%, fix the Pixelda crash and rebuild, and keep the incident open. Keep the flag ramp paused and the holdout running, or widen it, to settle whether the flag adds a few tenths of a point of memory kills. Don't roll back the crash-reporting SDK, because that would hide crashes. Confidence is high on the build cause and moderate on the flag's small effect.

The evidence does not support the claim as drafted. The shared RFI platform has audit timestamps users can't edit. Measured from submission, the architect answered 62 of 64 RFIs within the contract period. The two late ones were minor finishes queries that Callerby itself marked as having no programme impact. Of the 41 RFIs the claim calls late, 39 sat in Callerby's own draft status for 9–47 days. The claim's "late information" case rests on the wrong start date, so the 9-week element looks unsound.

The architect's register shows that only CO-09 (6 Nov 2025) touched the structure. The other five change orders were interior items. The crane left in October, before CO-09 was issued. Callerby's own people confirm it went to Kestrel and the frame crew went with it, and that levels 3–4 steel was on site. The likeliest main driver is Callerby's own redeployment. CO-09 may justify a smaller extension, and I can't size that from what I have. Fenmore earns 6% of any sums recovered.

Next steps:
- Don't submit the claim as drafted. Submitting figures you now have reason to doubt is risky.
- Don't withdraw it outright yet.
- Commission an independent delay analysis, focused on CO-09's real effect.
- Don't discipline the superintendent, who answered honestly.
- Review how the Kestrel incentive and crane transfers are governed, but don't suspend the scheme until the evidence ties it to the transfer.

The jump in write-offs comes mainly from inside the DC, not from Haverlow. Since the night receiving team was cut from six to four (27 July), chilled pallets wait about 3 h 52 min on an unrefrigerated dock, instead of 44 min. The dock averages 15–17°C overnight. Night write-off rates rose from 0.6% to 2.9% for every supplier, Pellridge and own-label included. Haverlow's trailer data shows product at 2.4–3.5°C when the doors open, with no trend. The 6.5–8°C receipt probes are keyed after the long dock wait, so they measure warming on site. The chambers are fine. A chargeback and volume move against Haverlow would punish the wrong party and leave the cause in place. Do not drop the night probe either, because that would hide the problem. Restore night receiving staff, or otherwise cut dock-to-chamber time, and set a maximum time monitored weekly from scan data. Separately, a smaller part of the rise is in customer credits. These roughly doubled after Corriebank's self-certified claims began on 3 August. Whether any claims are inflated is not established. Sample Corriebank's claims against lots before changing credit terms. I'm confident in the main diagnosis. The credit question is still open.

The rise in delayed alarm responses is most likely caused by the 12 August move of the alert relay server, not by agency nurses. The import skipped 11 of 14 forwarding rules. These included the 15-second hold-off for brief oxygen dips, suppression of repeats, and routing of probe-off alarms to the charge phone only. IT's smoke test checked only two beds and passed. Pods A-C now send about twice as many phone notifications per nurse (79-86 versus 37-39 per shift) and acknowledgement times doubled. Pod D, still on the old server, shows no change. Bedside alarm volume was flat, so acuity and the monitor update (23-24 September) don't explain it. Incident rates rose equally for core, agency and new-graduate nurses, so nurse experience is not the driver. The extra sick leave is probably from the viral season, though alarm overload may add to it. Do not approve the agency cap or the performance reviews. They would punish the wrong people and discourage reporting. Restore the 14 rules after Clinical Engineering validates them, with committee sign-off. Then track notifications per nurse and acknowledgement times weekly. Do not turn off phone forwarding of SpO2 or technical alarms. Wireless coverage is unlikely to be the cause, but the unit's reports that Room 14 phones don't ring are unexplained and worth a check. I'm fairly confident in this diagnosis.

The rejections were caused by our own paperwork, not by the fungicide, Lower Serra growers or Meridane. When Meridane bookings moved to the new Tallis system, the mandarin product record was copied from the avocado record on 1 Aug. It kept avocado's 7.0°C carriage temperature, where our specification is 4.0°C. All five Meridane containers were sent at 7.0°C and all were rejected, with decay of 9–14%. The four containers sent at 4.0°C, which were the Coastway ones plus the early Meridane K1, passed. That includes Pellacor-treated K5 and K7. Meridane's controller logs show the units held 7.0°C as instructed, so a refrigeration claim would fail. Lower Serra fruit was worse within the rejected containers, but it was only 28–40% of each container, and nobody has surveyed the accepted ones. That is a minor factor and does not justify suspending those growers or withholding their pay. Next steps: correct the temperature on the mandarin product record now, get Meridane to reset the container at sea and the one queued for 10 Oct to 4.0°C, and add a check of reefer settings against the specification before bookings are submitted. Do not switch fungicide back, suspend growers, or file the claim. Check the Tallis template for other products too. I'm quite confident in this, though a lab report could add detail.

Add a check comparing booking temperature with the product specification. Don't suspend Lower Serra, don't claim against Meridane, and don't revert the fungicide. Loggers in containers are a reasonable extra safeguard.

Don't pay the group-wide retention payment and close the review. It would cost about £228k, aim at the wrong cause, and end the inquiry. Run the confidential outside interviews (about £9k, three weeks), designed to separate workload from supervision. Add matter and supervising-partner fields to attrition tracking. Decide on contract reviewers or a change of supervisor after the interviews. Confidence is moderate: high that the problem is Kestrel-specific, low on which factor drives it.

Resignations are concentrated in the Kestrel team: 8 of 11 Kestrel associates left, against 1 of 13 other associates in the group. Other groups look normal, and the billable-target rise applied firm-wide, so neither it nor general market mobility explains this. Pay is probably not the main driver, since the Kestrel/non-Kestrel split is so lopsided, though pay may play a smaller part. I can't yet separate the heavy Kestrel workload from Dorian Faulk's supervision: all 11 Kestrel associates reported to him and he supervises no one else. The survey comments point to both. The exit forms are weak evidence because leavers knew the group head might read them. I'd advise against the £12k group-wide payment and closing the review. It would not address the concentration and would end the inquiry. Commission the confidential external interviews (about £9k, three weeks), structured to separate workload from supervision. Meanwhile, add matter and supervising partner to attrition reporting. Hold off on moving supervision or funding contract reviewers until the interviews show which cause matters. Confidence in the concentration finding is high. Confidence on supervision versus workload is low.

The rejects come from an interaction. Arnholt resin arrives wetter than Quillan, about 0.27–0.33% water against 0.11–0.14%. Dryer D7 handles it, with an outlet reading of 0.07%. Dryer D5 has degraded: its dew point is −16 to −19 instead of −40, and its alarm limit was loosened in week 31. D5 can't dry Arnholt below the 0.20% limit, so wet resin reaches Press 5. Press 5 with Arnholt rejects about 10% of parts. Press 5 with Quillan runs at 0.9%, and Press 7 with either resin runs at about 0.7–0.8%. One lot dried in a clean portable dryer gave 0.8% rejects on Press 5, against 10.4% through D5.

The new operators are not the cause. Their reject rates match the experienced operators' on both resins. Second shift looks worse only because all of its VX runs on Press 5, which now takes the Arnholt lots. Do not put the six on improvement plans, and do not drop Arnholt entirely.

This week:
1. Repair D5 and confirm its dew point is back at −40.
2. Restore the original alarm limit.
3. Keep Arnholt off D5 until that is verified.
4. Check moisture at the press throat for every resin lot.

The cause of the wetter Arnholt resin is still open. The north annex storage is a plausible reason but is not tested, so don't pay to move the resin yet. Confidence is high.

The rejects come from one combination: Arnholt resin dried in Press 5's dryer (D5), which is degraded. Arnholt on Press 5 rejects about 9.9%. Arnholt on Press 7 rejects 0.8%. Quillan on Press 5 rejects 0.9%. Neither the supplier nor the dryer fails alone. Arnholt arrives wetter, 0.27–0.33% moisture against 0.11–0.14% for Quillan. D5, with a dew point of about −16 to −19 °C, can't dry it below the 0.20% limit. The same Arnholt lot dried in a good dryer gave 0.8% rejects. The same lot through D5 gave 10.4%. One caveat: Arnholt was only stored in the north annex, so we can't say whether storage adds to the wetness. Next steps: repair D5 and restore its alarm limit. Keep Arnholt off D5 until the dew point is verified. Check feed-throat moisture on every lot. Give the customer's 8D this cause. Test conditioned storage separately.

Cancelling RotaWeave would probably not fix this. The drop is concentrated at Dock Street and Westgate, which lost their coordinator on 1 May and also use the app. Millbrook has the app but kept its coordinator, and it is nearly flat (118 to 111). Quarry Lane lost its coordinator but is not on the app, and it is also nearly flat (86 to 80). So neither change alone explains the fall. Together they do.

The app's basic tier has no recurring bookings. A regular keeps a weekly slot only if staff book it before Thursday's release. Staff bookings at Dock Street and Westgate fell from 74 a week to 3 after the coordinator left, and one admin seat sits unused. Of 213 April regulars at those two sites, 129 lost their usual slot at least twice, and 88% of those are now inactive. Among the 61 volunteers reached by phone, 44 said nobody booked them.

The background check is not the cause. 21 of the 23 people deactivated were reactivated, and 121 of the 123 who lapsed held a current check. Commonplate looks minor: only 2 of the 61 callbacks joined another group.

Next steps: assign someone to book regulars into their usual slots at Dock Street and Westgate before each Thursday release, and phone lapsed regulars to offer their slot back. Keep the background check, keep the contract for now, and do not remove inactive people from the roster or the retention figures. Confidence is fairly high. The main gap is that the callback sample is small.

Phone lapsed regulars to offer their slot back, and review after 60 days. Also plan this before Quarry Lane goes live on 6 Oct. Do not remove inactive volunteers from the figures. I am fairly confident in this, though the callback sample is small.

The drop is almost certainly not caused by Android 6.14. On 3 March at 10:38 UTC, Corvane's automatic rule-pack update added a rule (AUTO-LIB-17). It blocks password-login requests from the nettle-http library, which every Android app version uses. About 9,600 requests a day are blocked with a 403. The blocked requests come from about 41,300 install IDs, 92% of which logged in successfully in the previous 90 days, so they look like real customers rather than bots. The failures began within a minute on every app version, including 6.11 and older. They appear equally with and without the March OS patch. Quick-unlock, iOS and web are unaffected. Password success on Android fell from 96% to 8%.

What to do: don't roll back 6.14, and don't raise bot sensitivity. Raising it would block more real customers. Don't exclude blocked attempts from the KPI, because that would hide a real customer-facing failure. Instead, ask Corvane to put the rules added in 2026.03.1 into log-only mode on the mobile password path, keeping rate limits, lockout and other rules active. Then confirm in telemetry that password success returns to about 96%. Remaining uncertainty: the contact-centre call rise is only loosely tied to the login failures.

The Android 6.14 release is not the cause, so a rollback would not help. The drop comes from a new Corvane edge rule, AUTO-LIB-17. It came in with the vendor's 3 March rule-pack update and went live at 10:38 UTC. It blocks Android password logins because the app's networking library, nettle-http, looks like an automation tool. Customers are being blocked with HTTP 403, and the first block was at 10:41 UTC.

Evidence:
- The failures began within a minute on every app version, including versions that did not change.
- They hit every OS version, with or without the March security patch.
- Quick-unlock, iOS and web are unaffected.
- About 41,300 real installs were blocked, and 92% of them had logged in successfully before.
- Android password success fell from 96% to 8%.

The credential-stuffing theory and the 3 March token-lifetime change don't fit this pattern.

Next steps:
1. Ask Corvane today to set that one rule to log-only on the Android password path. Keep rate limits, lockout and all other rules on.
2. Confirm in login telemetry that Android password success recovers.
3. Do not raise bot-protection sensitivity, and do not drop blocked attempts from the KPI. Doing either would hide the problem or block more customers.
4. Drop the rollback plan and let the 6.14 rollout continue, but watch the numbers by version.
5. The call-volume rise is partly the fee mailing, so treat the link to the login drop as unproven.

I'm confident in this diagnosis.

Larger adjustments now go automatically to the Billing Resolution team. The share of billing calls referred rose from 7% to 54% in the same week. Referred calls resolve at about 33%, and non-referred calls still resolve at 82%, both unchanged. Billing resolution fell from 79% to 56%, while other call types barely moved. The tariff rise added tariff calls, but those resolve at 85%, so it isn't the cause. The IVR change came later, on 28 April, and FCR had already dropped. Workload isn't supported either. I'm fairly sure of this (about 85–90%). Next steps: don't put the April intake on performance plans, since that would penalise the wrong group. Agree a higher credit limit with Finance and trial it on two teams for six weeks, with post-call sampling of credits. That is what Finance's controller said they would consider. Track FCR and the unsupported-credit rate before any wider rollout. Don't pause the IVR work on this evidence.

The enrolment drop does not appear to be the Admissions Office's fault. Yield (the share of admitted students who enrolled) fell from 41.8% to 34.3%, while applications and admits rose, so the pool was not the problem. The drop is concentrated in the scholarship tiers where awards were cut: Dean's awards went from $14,000 to $9,000 and yield fell from 45.2% to 31.9%. Merit awards went from $9,000 to $5,000 and yield fell from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential awards and the no-award group, where nothing changed, were flat. Early-action students got decisions on time on the old system, and their yield fell by almost the same amount as regular-decision yield (7.4 vs 7.5 points). So late decisions do not explain the fall. The portal delays were real and probably cost some individual students, but the data show no measurable effect on the overall number. I'm fairly confident, though the tier data don't split early action from regular decision. Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee with a costed proposal to restore awards in the affected tiers before award letters go out. Separately, set a turnaround target for regular decisions and restore reader capacity. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the missing-transcript claims are checked.

Don't roll back the gateway. The latency jump comes from the storage compaction tuning pushed on the evening of 2 Nov. Compaction threads went from 2 to 6, disks went to about 97% busy within 5 minutes in every cell, and node-side read time rose from 61 to 262 ms. Per cell, p99 rose minutes after that push, not when each cell's gateway upgrade arrived. For example, use-1 got 5.8 at 22:05 but only degraded at 23:40, right after the push. The cell that skipped the push (aps-3) got 5.8 and stayed at about 94 ms. Rolling euw-1 back to 5.7 changed nothing. Network and traffic growth don't explain the pattern. Rolling back would reopen the security hole and wouldn't fix latency. Next step: revert the compaction tuning in one cell, watch p99 and backlog, then extend it if it works. Backlog is about 4% and projected to stay under 15% until at least 13 Nov, so there is room to do this carefully. Do not pause compaction fleet-wide. Hold off on rate-limiting Orrin until the 10 Nov backlog attribution is in. Confidence is high on the cause and lower on what drove the backlog growth.

The rise at store 14 may not be real. Its figures are interim estimates taken from partial cycle counts. Those estimates carry about ±0.6 points of error per quarter. In past years, about half of the stores that showed two straight rises had them rejected by the year-end full count. Store 14's own full counts have stayed at 1.5–1.8%. The shoplifting incident log is also unreliable as a trend. A chain-wide incident app launched on 1 April, and recorded incidents rose across the chain while chain shrink stayed flat. The neighbouring stores 9 and 22 show no rise, which is consistent with a store-specific issue, but it doesn't separate self-checkout from other causes. The ethics tip was checked on CCTV and showed only cardboard bale runs. The sales mix is stable, so it doesn't explain the rise. I have not shown that self-checkout, shoplifting or staff theft caused anything. My confidence is moderate.

Next steps: keep store 14 in the 7 December full count and reject the proposal to drop it. Dropping it would remove the one measurement that settles the question. Don't pull the self-checkout lanes, hire a guard, or suspend the stocker yet. After the count, compare it with the interim figures and then choose the response. If the loss is confirmed, look at self-checkout and the front end first.

Store 14's rising shrink is not yet shown to be a real rise in losses. The figures are interim estimates taken from partial cycle counts. They carry a margin of about ±0.6 points per quarter, and two-quarter rises like this one were confirmed by the year-end count only about half the time (13 of 27). Store 14's own full-count shrink has stayed at 1.5–1.8% for three years. The shoplifting log count is not reliable evidence of more theft: the incident app launched chain-wide on 1 April, and recorded incidents rose across the chain while chain shrink stayed flat. The tip about the night stocker was checked against CCTV and found to be bale runs, so there is nothing to support it. A change in sales mix does not explain the rise. Self-checkout, customer theft and a rise in estimate error all remain open. Neighbouring stores without self-checkout show no similar rise, which weakly hints at something local, but it does not settle the cause.

What to do: keep store 14 in the 7 December full count, which is the one measurement that can settle this. Do not drop the store from the count. Do not hire a guard, pull the lanes or discipline anyone until the count is compared with the interim figures. Then plan on the real result. I'm fairly confident in this, though not about the underlying cause.

The rise from 0.31% to 0.41% is very likely ordinary week-to-week variation, so I would not roll back. The last 26 weeks average 0.354% with an upper band edge of 0.482%. This week's 0.411% sits inside that band. Three earlier weeks were higher (0.44, 0.47 and 0.51%) and nothing was found when they were investigated. The burn-rate page did not fire (0.82x against a 2x threshold). The dashboard count matches a recount from the raw logs. Booking completion didn't change (41.0% to 41.2%), and support logged no complaints.

The "new pods error at twice the rate" figure is a rollout warm-up effect. Every recent rollout shows it, including a config-only redeploy of an unchanged image. Cold caches cause timeouts, but they add only 10–20 errors per rollout. That can't explain about 2,300 extra errors, and the comparison never matched pods of the same age.

What to do: record the week at ops review as within the normal band. Keep all alerting on, and do not mute it. Apply the standard check to next week. If the week of 2 Nov goes above the band, investigate then. I did not test the replica move or partner-sync month-end traffic, so those stay open. Confidence is fairly high.

The 5.2 release went live on 9 Oct, the same day as the cutover, which is why the two looked identical on the country-level dashboard. The handball launch came later and didn't change the stall rate, so it isn't the cause. ISP congestion doesn't fit either, since other clients on those ISPs are fine.

Recommendation: don't send the breach notice, withhold fees or roll back to Corvane. Don't mute the alert. Have the app team revert 5.2's adaptive-streaming behaviour in Kestria to the 5.1 settings and pause the wider 5.2 rollout until fixed. Then add app-version and device breakdowns to the dashboard and alerts. Hold off on the free-month offer for cancellers. The 1 Oct price rise also fits the cancellation increase, so buffering isn't shown to be the driver. Confidence is high on the cause, moderate on cancellations.

The complaints most likely come from contaminated brake fluid, not from drivers, the new pads, or the hills. During the bay closure, Northfield changed the fluid in 13 Eastgate vans. Eleven of them used fluid from one old bulk drum that had a missing cap and had taken on water. The two vans that got fluid from a new drum have no complaints. All 11 complaining vans are among those 11 bulk-drum vans. When Northfield retested two of these vans on 24 Sep, the fluid boiled at about 150°C, against 255°C for sealed stock. Wet fluid can vaporise on long descents and make the pedal soft. Drivers who reported faults in the affected vans had no reports in other vans, including on Upper Wend, and Calder Road's vans fitted with Tessaro pads had no complaints. Do not discipline drivers or retrain everyone on this basis. Doing so would punish the people raising a real safety issue. This week: take the 11 bulk-drum vans off the road, test their fluid, and renew it from sealed stock. Also check the other two Northfield vans, and ask Calder Road for its fluid records. The pad supplier switch needs no action yet. I'm fairly confident, though the Calder fluid source and the wider noise reports remain unchecked.

The director's plan would punish the wrong people and leave the fault in place. Don't do it.

Next: reset the Veltranol record, extend the hold to every Veltranol lot packed since 4 Oct (including the two Line 1 lots), add a second-person check of printed expiry against the batch record at each setup, and inspect other products edited in October. Two other products have future-dated edits and are unchecked. Also have the vendor and IT explain how PackBridge picked up a future-dated value. Keep the camera check on.
